cases.subject: introduction
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | Before you begin | Before you begin |  | This material is a learning aid to help you understand Swedish driving theory. It is not an official source and cannot replace official information from Trafikverket and Transportstyrelsen. Always consult their current guidance and the applicable rules. |  | This book is for English-speaking learners preparing for ordinary Swedish category B driving. It connects rules with decisions you can explain and practise. It does not grant permission to drive, replace mandatory training or supervised practice, reproduce official examination questions, or guarantee a test result. | How to use this book |  | Begin with modules 1–3. They establish personal readiness, vehicle preparation and road interpretation. Use modules 4–7 to apply that foundation in traffic and changing conditions. Modules 8–9 develop responsibility for the vehicle, its load and the journey's impact. Module 10 brings the learning together. |  | Each lesson contains a goal, an explanation, an original worked situation, a knowledge check with its answer, and a short reminder. After each module, write a reflection and use it to plan your next study or supervised practice session. Explain the answer before reading it; then change one condition in the example and consider whether your decision would change. | Sources

cases.subject: study-guide
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | How to use this book | Read, reflect and practise | Read the labels |  | Requirements describe applicable duties or conditions, with official references. Official recommendations/advice describe the named authority's guidance. Learning approaches, worked decisions and review guides are original teaching material. They help you apply the principles; they are not additional laws. English explanations are written for learning and do not replace the Swedish legal wording. | Use the official references |  | References appear beside factual material. Trafikverket and Transportstyrelsen provide the main guidance. Official legislation and other public authorities supply details missing from the main agency guidance. Selected manufacturer handbooks supply missing technical cautions and are listed separately. The lessons identify source limits and distinguish recommendations, research and teaching inferences from legal duties. Use the handbook for the actual vehicle; a generic example is not its operating procedure. | Check current guidance |  | Original licensing, examination and vehicle checks are dated 1 October 2026; added passages have their own checks on 12–13 October. Check current official information before using a time-sensitive rule. Hypothetical numbers in examples are identified as such and are not measurements of your vehicle or personal performance. | Sources

cases.subject: M01
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | Choose to drive responsibly |  | Driving begins with a choice: whether this person, this vehicle and this journey are ready to go together. Sweden’s Vision Zero (Nollvisionen) aims for no one to be killed or seriously injured in traffic. The choices taught here contribute to that aim. Trafikverket: Vision Zero Learning rules matters, but so does recognising when a different plan is safer. This module helps you build both habits. |  | In this chapter |  | M01-L01 · Your route into driving |  |  | M01-L02 · Am I ready today? |  |  | M01-L03 · Pressure is a driving risk |  |  | M01-L04 · Plan the journey before the ignition |  |  | M01-R · Review and self-assessment |  |  | This material is a learning aid to help you understand Swedish driving theory. It is not an official source and cannot replace official information from Trafikverket and Transportstyrelsen. Always consult their current guidance and the applicable rules. |  | Original sources checked 4 October 2026; G1 additions checked 12 October 2026. Consult current official guidance and applicable rules. | Sources | Nollvisionen – tillsammans räddar vi liv | Next: Your route into driving

cases.subject: M01-L01
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 1. Choose to drive responsibly | Your route into driving |  | Your goal: Build a personal preparation checklist covering entitlement, permits, supervised practice, risk training and examinations. |  | Requirements. For an ordinary new category B licence, you need a valid learner permit, permanent residence in Sweden or at least six months of study here, the minimum age of 18, valid car risk training, and successful theory and practical tests. Holding another EEA licence affects the application route. Category B normally covers a passenger car or light goods vehicle with a registered maximum weight of no more than 3,500 kg; trailers are explained in module 8. Check any conditions on your entitlement, including an automatic-transmission restriction. Transportstyrelsen: category B |  |  | Private practice requires an approved supervisor for the particular learner. The learner normally needs a group 1 permit. Practice in a passenger car can begin at 16; the minimum is 17 years and 6 months for practice with a light goods vehicle or a light trailer. The supervisor is legally treated as the driver, must carry proof of approval, and the practice sign must be clearly visible from behind. Exceptions concerning an existing entitlement must be checked against your own circumstances. Transportstyrelsen: category B |  |  | Current changes, checked 1 October 2026. The introductory-course requirement for private practice ended on 1 August 2026. Supervisor approval still applies. This change does not remove mandatory risk training. A theory test passed on or after 19 August 2026 is valid for one year. Tests passed before that date retain the earlier rules; Trafikverket describes the ordinary earlier validity as four months. Check your own result and any approved extension rather than adding a year yourself. Supervisor requirements · Risk training · Test validity amendment · Trafikverket: B tests |  |  |  |  | Apply the learning |  | Risk training has two parts: the first covers alcohol, drugs, fatigue and other risky behaviour; the second covers speed, safety and differing road/weather conditions, including slippery-road training. It must be completed before the tests and remains valid until the licence is obtained or for at most five years. Car and motorcycle risk training are not interchangeable. Transportstyrelsen: risk training |  |  | Build your checklist. Record your permit, supervisor approval if practising privately, entitlement conditions, risk-training status, test preparation and any support application. Use actual expiry dates from your records. Schedule practice around skills you need to improve, not only around an available test slot. |  | Worked decision. Noor plans to practise privately in September 2026. Her relative says no approvals are needed because a course was abolished. Noor checks the current supervisor page and waits for supervisor approval. The removed course and the retained approval are different requirements. |  |  | Knowledge check. Does a theory pass from July 2026 automatically become valid for a year? | Show answer |  | Remember: Plan the administrative route and the learning route together. | Sources | Transportstyrelsen: category B | Supervisor requirements | Risk training | Test validity amendment | Trafikverket: B tests | Previous: Choose to drive responsibly | Next: Am I ready today?

cases.subject: M01-L02
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 1. Choose to drive responsibly | Am I ready today? |  | Your goal: Decide whether to drive when tiredness, illness, medication, alcohol or drugs may affect you, and explain a safer alternative. |  | Requirement. You must not drive when illness, exhaustion, alcohol, other substances or another condition prevents safe control. A legal alcohol threshold is not a guarantee that you are capable of driving safely. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §1 |  |  | Trafikverket states that the blood-alcohol limit for drink-driving is 0.2 per mille. For an aggravated offence, factors include at least 1.0 per mille, substantial impairment, or driving that creates a clear traffic danger. Non-prescribed narcotics are subject to a zero-tolerance rule. Properly prescribed medication does not make impaired driving acceptable. Trafikverket: drink-driving law · Alcohol, drugs and medication |  |  |  | Alcohol can affect judgement, attention, vision, reactions and coordination. Feeling normal does not measure those effects. Performance can remain impaired the next day. Do not use a fixed number of hours, a shower, coffee or a calculation as a personal clearance to drive. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist about medicines and driving; do not change a prescribed treatment simply to make a journey. Trafikverket: effects of alcohol and medicines |  |  | Learning approach. Before taking the keys, ask: Can I stay alert? Can I see and move well enough? Has anything changed since I last drove? Can I concentrate on several developing situations? If the answers are uncertain, make a different travel plan and resolve the uncertainty first. Medical eligibility and day-to-day readiness are related but different: having a licence does not mean you are fit for every journey. Medical requirements |  | Sleep and safe judgement |  | Medical explanation · Sleep and awareness. Microsleep (mikrosömn) is a brief, unintended episode of sleep. You do not choose it or reliably prevent it by deciding to try harder. For a deliberately hypothetical two-second lapse at a constant 90 km/h, distance = speed × time: 90 ÷ 3.6 = 25 metres per second; 25 × 2 = 50 metres travelled while asleep. Two seconds is an example, not a prediction of how long a microsleep lasts. CDC/NIOSH: microsleeps |  |  | Official safety advice · Replace missing sleep with sleep. Adequate sleep is the fundamental remedy for sleep deprivation. Coffee or an energy drink may briefly make you feel more alert, but does not replace the sleep you need; serious sleep deprivation can still lead to microsleep. Music, an open window or willpower should not be treated as a clearance to drive: they do not provide the missing sleep. Do not start when you cannot stay awake; if sleepiness develops, stop somewhere safe and arrange rest or another way to travel. See M07-L03 for planning around fatigue on a journey. NHTSA: drowsy driving |  |  |  | Medical explanation · Stimulation is not safe judgement. Stimulant misuse, for example involving amphetamine or cocaine, can produce overconfidence while judgement and concentration are impaired. Some stimulant effects can reduce the feeling of fatigue or drowsiness: tiredness may be masked rather than the need for sleep removed. Feeling energetic is therefore not proof of safe driving ability. Effects vary with substance, dose and individual circumstances; this does not mean every prescribed stimulant treatment has the same effect. Ask your prescriber about your treatment and driving. Swedish Government: stimulant confidence and judgement · NHTSA: stimulant effects |  |  |  | Practice example. Lina slept too little before an evening journey. She suggests an energy drink and loud music; her friend suggests a stimulant to make her feel confident. The missing sleep remains unresolved, and a stronger feeling of alertness cannot certify safe judgement. She postpones the drive or arranges an alert driver, and makes time for adequate sleep before driving again. | Apply the learning | A tired learner and a companion pause beside a parked car. The keys remain on the bench. |  | A tired learner and a companion pause beside a parked car. The keys remain on the bench. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked decision. A driver has taken a new medicine and feels unusually drowsy. A passenger offers to keep talking to help them stay awake. The safer choice is to arrange another driver or transport and ask for medication advice. Conversation does not resolve the impairment. |  |  | Knowledge check. (1) Is driving automatically acceptable if a medicine was prescribed correctly? (2) How does microsleep differ from choosing to close your eyes? (3) A sleep-deprived driver feels energetic and unusually confident after taking a stimulant. Has the missing sleep been remedied, and does that feeling establish safe judgement? | Show answer |  | Remember: Decide fitness before deciding convenience. | Sources | Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §1 | Trafikverket: drink-driving law | Alcohol, drugs and medication | Medical requirements | Microsleeps — Module 3, Negative Impacts on Sleep | Drowsy Driving | Drograttfylleri och sjöfylleri — proposition 1998/99:43 | Drugs and Human Performance Fact Sheets | Previous: Your route into driving | Next: Pressure is a driving risk

cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 1. Choose to drive responsibly | Am I ready today? |  | Your goal: Decide whether to drive when tiredness, illness, medication, alcohol or drugs may affect you, and explain a safer alternative. |  | Requirement. You must not drive when illness, exhaustion, alcohol, other substances or another condition prevents safe control. A legal alcohol threshold is not a guarantee that you are capable of driving safely. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §1 |  |  | Trafikverket states that the blood-alcohol limit for drink-driving is 0.2 per mille. For an aggravated offence, factors include at least 1.0 per mille, substantial impairment, or driving that creates a clear traffic danger. Non-prescribed narcotics are subject to a zero-tolerance rule. Properly prescribed medication does not make impaired driving acceptable. Trafikverket: drink-driving law · Alcohol, drugs and medication |  |  |  | Alcohol can affect judgement, attention, vision, reactions and coordination. Feeling normal does not measure those effects. Performance can remain impaired the next day. Do not use a fixed number of hours, a shower, coffee or a calculation as a personal clearance to drive. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist about medicines and driving; do not change a prescribed treatment simply to make a journey. Trafikverket: effects of alcohol and medicines |  |  | Learning approach. Before taking the keys, ask: Can I stay alert? Can I see and move well enough? Has anything changed since I last drove? Can I concentrate on several developing situations? If the answers are uncertain, make a different travel plan and resolve the uncertainty first. Medical eligibility and day-to-day readiness are related but different: having a licence does not mean you are fit for every journey. Medical requirements |  | Sleep and safe judgement |  | Medical explanation · Sleep and awareness. Microsleep (mikrosömn) is a brief, unintended episode of sleep. You do not choose it or reliably prevent it by deciding to try harder. For a deliberately hypothetical two-second lapse at a constant 90 km/h, distance = speed × time: 90 ÷ 3.6 = 25 metres per second; 25 × 2 = 50 metres travelled while asleep. Two seconds is an example, not a prediction of how long a microsleep lasts. CDC/NIOSH: microsleeps |  |  | Official safety advice · Replace missing sleep with sleep. Adequate sleep is the fundamental remedy for sleep deprivation. Coffee or an energy drink may briefly make you feel more alert, but does not replace the sleep you need; serious sleep deprivation can still lead to microsleep. Music, an open window or willpower should not be treated as a clearance to drive: they do not provide the missing sleep. Do not start when you cannot stay awake; if sleepiness develops, stop somewhere safe and arrange rest or another way to travel. See M07-L03 for planning around fatigue on a journey. Stimulant misuse, for example involving amphetamine or cocaine, can produce overconfidence while judgement and concentration are impaired. Some stimulant effects can reduce the feeling of fatigue or drowsiness: tiredness may be masked rather than the need for sleep removed. Feeling energetic is therefore not proof of safe driving ability. Effects vary with substance, dose and individual circumstances; this does not mean every prescribed stimulant treatment has the same effect. Ask your prescriber about your treatment and driving. Trafikverket: drink-driving law · Alcohol, drugs and medication |  |  |  | Alcohol can affect judgement, attention, vision, reactions and coordination. Feeling normal does not measure those effects. Performance can remain impaired the next day. Do not use a fixed number of hours, a shower, coffee or a calculation as a personal clearance to drive. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist about medicines and driving; do not change a prescribed treatment simply to make a journey. Trafikverket: effects of alcohol and medicines |  |  | Learning approach. Before taking the keys, ask: Can I stay alert? Can I see and move well enough? Has anything changed since I last drove? Can I concentrate on several developing situations? If the answers are uncertain, make a different travel plan and resolve the uncertainty first. Medical eligibility and day-to-day readiness are related but different: having a licence does not mean you are fit for every journey. Medical requirements |  | Sleep and safe judgement |  | Medical explanation · Sleep and awareness. Microsleep (mikrosömn) is a brief, unintended episode of sleep. You do not choose it or reliably prevent it by deciding to try harder. For a deliberately hypothetical two-second lapse at a constant 90 km/h, distance = speed × time: 90 ÷ 3.6 = 25 metres per second; 25 × 2 = 50 metres travelled while asleep. Two seconds is an example, not a prediction of how long a microsleep lasts. CDC/NIOSH: microsleeps |  |  | Official safety advice · Replace missing sleep with sleep. Adequate sleep is the fundamental remedy for sleep deprivation. Coffee or an energy drink may briefly make you feel more alert, but does not replace the sleep you need; serious sleep deprivation can still lead to microsleep. Music, an open window or willpower should not be treated as a clearance to drive: they do not provide the missing sleep. Do not start when you cannot stay awake; if sleepiness develops, stop somewhere safe and arrange rest or another way to travel. See M07-L03 for planning around fatigue on a journey. NHTSA: drowsy driving |  |  |  | Medical explanation · Stimulation is not safe judgement. Stimulant misuse, for example involving amphetamine or cocaine, can produce overconfidence while judgement and concentration are impaired. Some stimulant effects can reduce the feeling of fatigue or drowsiness: tiredness may be masked rather than the need for sleep removed. Feeling energetic is therefore not proof of safe driving ability. Effects vary with substance, dose and individual circumstances; this does not mean every prescribed stimulant treatment has the same effect. Ask your prescriber about your treatment and driving. Swedish Government: stimulant confidence and judgement · NHTSA: stimulant effects |  |  |  | Practice example. Lina slept too little before an evening journey. She suggests an energy drink and loud music; her friend suggests a stimulant to make her feel confident. The missing sleep remains unresolved, and a stronger feeling of alertness cannot certify safe judgement. She postpones the drive or arranges an alert driver, and makes time for adequate sleep before driving again. | Apply the learning | A tired learner and a companion pause beside a parked car. The keys remain on the bench. |  | A tired learner and a companion pause beside a parked car. The keys remain on the bench. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked decision. A driver has taken a new medicine and feels unusually drowsy. A passenger offers to keep talking to help them stay awake. The safer choice is to arrange another driver or transport and ask for medication advice. Conversation does not resolve the impairment. |  |  | Knowledge check. (1) Is driving automatically acceptable if a medicine was prescribed correctly? (2) How does microsleep differ from choosing to close your eyes? (3) A sleep-deprived driver feels energetic and unusually confident after taking a stimulant. Has the missing sleep been remedied, and does that feeling establish safe judgement? | Show answer |  | Remember: Decide fitness before deciding convenience. | Sources | Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §1 | Trafikverket: drink-driving law | Alcohol, drugs and medication | Medical requirements | Microsleeps — Module 3, Negative Impacts on Sleep | Drowsy Driving | Drograttfylleri och sjöfylleri — proposition 1998/99:43 | Drugs and Human Performance Fact Sheets | Previous: Your route into driving | Next: Pressure is a driving risk

cases.subject: M01-L03
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 1. Choose to drive responsibly | Pressure is a driving risk |  | Your goal: Identify how peers, impulses, confidence and personal circumstances can change a decision, and rehearse a refusal or alternative. |  | The official education syllabus asks learners to reflect on social influence, impulsive decisions, personal motives and their own limitations. These are skills to practise, not labels to attach to an age group or personality. Category B syllabus, chapter 5 |  |  | Learning approach. Separate the journey's purpose from the feeling of the moment. “Get everyone home” is a purpose. “Show that I can handle this bend quickly” is a different motive. When a passenger's request changes your speed, following distance or willingness to overtake, name the change before acting on it. |  | A useful personal boundary is a sentence you can use without debate: “I will stop somewhere safe before changing the route”; “I am not passing here”; or “We need another way home.” These are original rehearsal tools, not official scripts. Practise them before a difficult situation, and agree that passengers will help with navigation only when asked. |  | Requirement. You still owe care to other road users and must adapt speed to conditions. Cooperation does not authorise ignoring a traffic rule because another person is impatient. Traffic Regulation, chapter 2 §1 and chapter 3 §14 |  |  | Official policy aim · Vision Zero. Nollvisionen means no one should be killed or seriously injured in traffic. It is not a promise that nobody will ever make a mistake. Trafikverket describes shared responsibility: road users must show consideration and judgement and follow traffic rules, while system designers have ultimate responsibility for the system’s safety. Your part includes choosing safe speed and margins and refusing a pressured manoeuvre; road and vehicle design also contribute. For example, staying behind a vehicle near a hidden crest helps protect people even when a passenger dislikes the delay. Trafikverket: Vision Zero |  | Apply the learning | A passenger talks to the driver. In the road view, the car remains behind a van near a crest. Illustration, not a scale diagram of following distance. |  | A passenger talks to the driver. In the road view, the car remains behind a van near a crest. Illustration, not a scale diagram of following distance. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked decision. Friends laugh when Amir stays behind a slow vehicle on a road with a hidden crest. He recognises the urge to prove himself, maintains space and waits for a genuinely suitable opportunity. His decision protects the purpose of the trip: arriving safely. There is no need to “win” the interaction. |  |  | Knowledge check. (1) Which is better evidence of readiness: feeling confident, or repeatedly identifying hazards and responding safely during supervised practice? (2) Does Vision Zero aim only to reduce minor collisions, or to prevent deaths and serious injuries? | Show answer |  | Remember: A decision can be socially uncomfortable and still be the correct driving decision. | Sources | Nollvisionen – tillsammans räddar vi liv | Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §1 | Category B syllabus, chapter 5 | Previous: Am I ready today? | Next: Plan the journey before the ignition

cases.subject: M01-L04
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 1. Choose to drive responsibly | Plan the journey before the ignition |  | Your goal: Compare route, departure time, travel mode and passenger choices for safety, accessibility and environmental impact. |  | Official advice · Trafikverket |  | Trafikverket recommends checking forecasts and traffic conditions, allowing time, taking breaks on longer trips and preparing supplies appropriate to the season. The education syllabus also asks you to consider whether a car is the right means of transport and how passengers or timing affect a journey. Journey advice · Syllabus, chapters 4–5 |  |  |  | Learning approach. Plan a usable journey rather than an ideal arrival time. Check where you can rest, refuel or charge as appropriate to the vehicle, and stop legally at the destination. Arrange restraints and space for passengers before departure. If the route has unfamiliar junctions or restrictions, identify them while parked. |  | Compare realistic alternatives. Walking, cycling or public transport may suit some journeys; a car may be necessary for others. Consider access needs, luggage, the return trip and the conditions at the time you will actually travel. A plan that depends on rushing after a late appointment is already fragile. | Apply the learning | Viewed over their shoulders, two people study a digital map on a tablet facing them. Rain falls outside. The map is illustrative, not live route guidance. |  | Viewed over their shoulders, two people study a digital map on a tablet facing them. Rain falls outside. The map is illustrative, not live route guidance. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked decision. A learner and supervisor can practise on a familiar route in daylight or travel through an unfamiliar town during a forecast snow shower. They choose daylight practice today and plan a later lesson for more demanding conditions with suitable preparation. This is staged learning, not an assumption that difficult conditions can always be avoided. |  |  | Knowledge check. You are delayed before leaving. What should change first: the arrival expectation or the safety margin? | Show answer |  | Remember: Keep a fallback plan that does not depend on taking extra risk. | Sources | Category B syllabus, chapter 5 | Journey advice | Previous: Pressure is a driving risk | Next: Review and self-assessment

Choose to drive responsibly | Plan the journey before the ignition |  | Your goal: Compare route, departure time, travel mode and passenger choices for safety, accessibility and environmental impact. |  | Official advice · Trafikverket |  | Trafikverket recommends checking forecasts and traffic conditions, allowing time, taking breaks on longer trips and preparing supplies appropriate to the season. The education syllabus also asks you to consider whether a car is the right means of transport and how passengers or timing affect a journey. Journey advice · Syllabus, chapters 4–5 |  |  |  | Learning approach. Plan a usable journey rather than an ideal arrival time. Check where you can rest, refuel or charge as appropriate to the vehicle, and stop legally at the destination. Arrange restraints and space for passengers before departure. If the route has unfamiliar junctions or restrictions, identify them while parked. |  | Compare realistic alternatives. Walking, cycling or public transport may suit some journeys; a car may be necessary for others. Consider access needs, luggage, the return trip and the conditions at the time you will actually travel. A plan that depends on rushing after a late appointment is already fragile. | Apply the learning | Viewed over their shoulders, two people study a digital map on a tablet facing them. Rain falls outside. The map is illustrative, not live route guidance. |  | Viewed over their shoulders, two people study a digital map on a tablet facing them. Rain falls outside. The map is illustrative, not live route guidance. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked decision. A learner and supervisor can practise on a familiar route in daylight or travel through an unfamiliar town during a forecast snow shower. They choose daylight practice today and plan a later lesson for more demanding conditions with suitable preparation. This is staged learning, not an assumption that difficult conditions can always be avoided. |  |  | Knowledge check. You are delayed before leaving. What should change first: the arrival expectation or the safety margin? | Show answer |  | Remember: Keep a fallback plan that does not depend on taking extra risk. | Sources | Category B syllabus, chapter 5 | Journey advice | Previous: Pressure is a driving risk | Next: Review and self-assessment

cases.subject: M02-L01
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 2. Prepare a car that is ready | Know what the controls tell you |  | Your goal: Explain the purpose of core controls, warning indicators, braking and steering systems, and identify when further instructions are needed. |  | The practical test can include checking steering, brakes, tyres, lighting, fluids and warning systems. You should be able to explain why you check them and propose action if you find a problem. Before moving, adjust the seat, head restraint, steering wheel, mirrors and belt. Trafikverket: safety check |  |  | Learning approach. While parked, locate the service brake, parking brake, transmission controls, indicators, lighting controls, wipers, washers, demisting and hazard lights. Explain what each control is for, then demonstrate it with your supervisor. “I can find it” and “I can use it without losing attention” are different learning stages. |  | The service brake is used to reduce speed and stop; the parking brake helps secure a stationary vehicle. Steering changes the vehicle's direction, but the tyres and road must provide the forces needed to follow that direction. Braking and steering share the available friction: turning the wheel is not proof that the car can follow the intended path. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§14 and 50 · VTI friction report, section 4.3 |  |  |  | Vehicle-specific boundary. Control layouts, warning meanings and system checks differ. Use the instructions for the actual vehicle before trying an unfamiliar function. This material does not prescribe a universal brake-servo test, fluid-opening procedure or response to every dashboard symbol. An unexplained warning is a reason to establish what is wrong before treating the car as ready. | Brakes and protective circuits |  | Technical explanation · Brakes and electrical protection. Separate brake circuits provide a reserve: if one circuit fails, the remaining circuit can still provide some braking. This reduces the chance of losing all braking through one circuit fault. Remaining braking may be weaker; it is not permission to continue normally. The technical requirements distinguish the surviving capability from full service-brake performance. Transportstyrelsen: brake circuits |  |  | ABS in an emergency. Anti-lock braking helps prevent wheel locking and can preserve steering control. During an emergency stop with ABS, keep firm, continuous pressure on the brake pedal and steer as necessary; do not pump the pedal. Pulsation or vibration through the pedal during ABS operation can be normal feedback as the system regulates braking. This differs from a changed pedal feel in ordinary braking. ABS does not guarantee a shorter stop or create grip that the tyres lack. UK Government: ABS instruction, Rule 120 · Ford: normal ABS feedback, 2011 Explorer |  |  |  | Recognise a symptom, then act. The table gives possibilities, not diagnoses. A sinking pedal can suggest internal leakage, although some servo/pump behaviour can resemble it. Air can cause hydraulic pedal sponginess. Obtain professional assessment for an unexplained change. Transportstyrelsen: brake inspection · Northern Ireland government: vehicle faults |  |  |  |  | Symptom |  | Pulsating pedal during an emergency ABS stop |  | Possible cause |  | Normal ABS operation |  | Action |  | Keep firm continuous pressure; steer as needed. |  |  | Symptom |  | Pedal slowly sinks under steady pressure |  | Possible cause |  | Hydraulic leakage or another brake fault |  | Action |  | Do not start an unsafe journey; obtain professional help. |  |  | Symptom |  | Hydraulic pedal feels unusually springy or spongy |  | Possible cause |  | Air in the brake system |  | Action |  | Have it checked before moving; do not rely on normal braking. |  |  | Symptom |  | Steering vibrates at certain speeds |  | Possible cause |  | Wheel imbalance; other faults are possible |  | Action |  | Have tyres, wheels and steering assessed; see M02-L02. |  |  | What a fuse does. A fuse protects an electrical circuit by interrupting excessive current during an overload or short circuit. Investigate faults under the actual vehicle's instructions. Transportstyrelsen: fuse protection principle |  | Apply the learning | A learner consults the vehicle handbook beside a parked car. Establish the actual controls before driving; no universal dashboard layout is shown. |  | A learner consults the vehicle handbook beside a parked car. Establish the actual controls before driving; no universal dashboard layout is shown. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked decision. Leila starts a borrowed car and sees a warning she cannot identify. Instead of driving to see whether it disappears, she stays parked, consults the vehicle instructions and seeks help. The lesson is to resolve uncertainty, not to guess from a warning's colour alone. |  |  | Knowledge check. (1) Does a familiar selector guarantee familiar operation? (2) Why separate brake circuits? (3) What should you do when the pedal pulsates during emergency ABS braking? (4) What might a sinking or unusually spongy pedal suggest? (5) What does a fuse protect against? | Show answer |  | Remember: Learn a function, its limitations and the appropriate response—not only its button. | Sources | Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §1 | Trafikverket: safety check | VTI friction report, section 4.3 | TSFS 2013:63 – vehicle technical requirements | The Highway Code – Rule 120 | 2011 Explorer Owner’s Guide | TSFS 2017:54 – control inspection | Taxi Driver Manual | Elektrisk utrustning och elinstallationer | Previous: Prepare a car that is ready | Next: A check before moving

cases.subject: M02-L01/goal
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 2. Prepare a car that is ready | Know what the controls tell you |  | Your goal: Explain the purpose of core controls, warning indicators, braking and steering systems, and identify when further instructions are needed. |  | The practical test can include checking steering, brakes, tyres, lighting, fluids and warning systems. You should be able to explain why you check them and propose action if you find a problem. Before moving, adjust the seat, head restraint, steering wheel, mirrors and belt. Trafikverket: safety check |  |  | Learning approach. While parked, locate the service brake, parking brake, transmission controls, indicators, lighting controls, wipers, washers, demisting and hazard lights. Explain what each control is for, then demonstrate it with your supervisor. “I can find it” and “I can use it without losing attention” are different learning stages. |  | The service brake is used to reduce speed and stop; the parking brake helps secure a stationary vehicle. Steering changes the vehicle's direction, but the tyres and road must provide the forces needed to follow that direction. Braking and steering share the available friction: turning the wheel is not proof that the car can follow the intended path. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§14 and 50 · VTI friction report, section 4.3 |  |  |  | Vehicle-specific boundary. Control layouts, warning meanings and system checks differ. Use the instructions for the actual vehicle before trying an unfamiliar function. This material does not prescribe a universal brake-servo test, fluid-opening procedure or response to every dashboard symbol. An unexplained warning is a reason to establish what is wrong before treating the car as ready. | Brakes and protective circuits |  | Technical explanation · Brakes and electrical protection. Separate brake circuits provide a reserve: if one circuit fails, the remaining circuit can still provide some braking. This reduces the chance of losing all braking through one circuit fault. Remaining braking may be weaker; it is not permission to continue normally. The technical requirements distinguish the surviving capability from full service-brake performance. Transportstyrelsen: brake circuits |  |  | ABS in an emergency. Anti-lock braking helps prevent wheel locking and can preserve steering control. During an emergency stop with ABS, keep firm, continuous pressure on the brake pedal and steer as necessary; do not pump the pedal. Pulsation or vibration through the pedal during ABS operation can be normal feedback as the system regulates braking. This differs from a changed pedal feel in ordinary braking. ABS does not guarantee a shorter stop or create grip that the tyres lack. UK Government: ABS instruction, Rule 120 · Ford: normal ABS feedback, 2011 Explorer |  |  |  | Recognise a symptom, then act. The table gives possibilities, not diagnoses. A sinking pedal can suggest internal leakage, although some servo/pump behaviour can resemble it. Air can cause hydraulic pedal sponginess. Obtain professional assessment for an unexplained change. Transportstyrelsen: brake inspection · Northern Ireland government: vehicle faults |  |  |  |  | Symptom |  | Pulsating pedal during an emergency ABS stop |  | Possible cause |  | Normal ABS operation |  | Action |  | Keep firm continuous pressure; steer as needed. |  |  | Symptom |  | Pedal slowly sinks under steady pressure |  | Possible cause |  | Hydraulic leakage or another brake fault |  | Action |  | Do not start an unsafe journey; obtain professional help. |  |  | Symptom |  | Hydraulic pedal feels unusually springy or spongy |  | Possible cause |  | Air in the brake system |  | Action |  | Have it checked before moving; do not rely on normal braking. |  |  | Symptom |  | Steering vibrates at certain speeds |  | Possible cause |  | Wheel imbalance; other faults are possible |  | Action |  | Have tyres, wheels and steering assessed; see M02-L02. |  |  | What a fuse does. A fuse protects an electrical circuit by interrupting excessive current during an overload or short circuit. Investigate faults under the actual vehicle's instructions. Transportstyrelsen: fuse protection principle |  | Apply the learning | A learner consults the vehicle handbook beside a parked car. Establish the actual controls before driving; no universal dashboard layout is shown. |  | A learner consults the vehicle handbook beside a parked car. Establish the actual controls before driving; no universal dashboard layout is shown. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked decision. Leila starts a borrowed car and sees a warning she cannot identify. Instead of driving to see whether it disappears, she stays parked, consults the vehicle instructions and seeks help. The lesson is to resolve uncertainty, not to guess from a warning's colour alone. |  |  | Knowledge check. (1) Does a familiar selector guarantee familiar operation? (2) Why separate brake circuits? (3) What should you do when the pedal pulsates during emergency ABS braking? (4) What might a sinking or unusually spongy pedal suggest? (5) What does a fuse protect against? | Show answer |  | Remember: Learn a function, its limitations and the appropriate response—not only its button. | Sources | Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §1 | Trafikverket: safety check | VTI friction report, section 4.3 | TSFS 2013:63 – vehicle technical requirements | The Highway Code – Rule 120 | 2011 Explorer Owner’s Guide | TSFS 2017:54 – control inspection | Taxi Driver Manual | Elektrisk utrustning och elinstallationer | Previous: Prepare a car that is ready | Next: A check before moving

cases.subject: M02-L02
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 2. Prepare a car that is ready | A check before moving |  | Your goal: Organise a safety check of tyres, lights, visibility and vehicle condition, and distinguish a defect from a reason to seek help. |  | Learning approach. Work around the car, then through the driving position. Look for damaged tyres, an unusual stance, leaks or obstructions; confirm that windows and mirrors permit a useful view. Check required lights and indicators, and ask for help where a second person is useful. Check washers and wipers before you need them in poor weather. Use the actual vehicle's instructions for fluid levels and service checks. These groups reflect the official practical-test safety check; they are not a guarantee that a quick walkaround detects every defect. Trafikverket: safety check |  |  | Requirements. Tyres must be suitable for the vehicle, including load capacity and applicable speed capability. The registration information and approved vehicle requirements matter when changing tyre sizes. Do not assume any wheel that physically fits is suitable. Transportstyrelsen: tyre requirements |  |  | Required lighting must work and be used appropriately. Some cars can run daytime lights without rear lights; the driver must ensure suitable front, rear and side lighting is on in darkness, twilight or poor weather. A trailer's lighting must be on during travel. Automatic settings may need manual intervention. Transportstyrelsen: vehicle lighting |  |  | Technical explanation · Steering vibration. Uneven mass distribution around a rotating wheel and tyre can cause steering vibration, sometimes most noticeable at particular speeds. Wheel imbalance is one possible cause, not a diagnosis: tyre damage and other wheel or steering defects may also be involved. Arrange assessment rather than testing the symptom by driving faster. Northern Ireland government: wheel balance and vehicle faults |  |  | Vehicle instructions · A temporary spare. Before using a temporary spare, read the actual car and spare-wheel instructions for maximum speed, distance or use restrictions, and required tyre pressure. Follow those limits and replace it with the normal wheel as instructed. Its pressure can differ from the road tyres. Volvo's 2019 V60 Twin Engine handbook gives one model's temporary-use, speed and pressure requirements; these cannot be assumed for every car. Volvo: temporary spare, 2019 V60 Twin Engine |  | Apply the learning | A companion checks the rear of a stationary car and trailer. Check the trailer lights directly before moving. |  | A companion checks the rear of a stationary car and trailer. Check the trailer lights directly before moving. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked decision. A passenger notices that the trailer's rear lights are dark although the car's daytime lights are on. cases.subject: M02-L03
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 2. Prepare a car that is ready | Protect everyone inside |  | Your goal: Select suitable restraints for passengers and explain how belts, headrests and airbags work together. |  | Requirements. In an ordinary car journey, occupants must use an available belt-equipped place and wear the belt. Children under 135 cm normally need an appropriate child restraint. The driver must take appropriate measures to ensure passengers under 15 use the required protection. Limited exceptions exist, including specified short occasional journeys, and should not become a routine travel plan. Seat-belt rules · Traffic Regulation, chapter 4 §§10–10d |  |  |  | For a child aged three or more but shorter than 135 cm, an occasional short transport without an available child restraint is an exception only under the stated conditions: use the belt where possible and not the front seat of a passenger car or light goods vehicle. For a child under three, the exception is an occasional short taxi trip, also excluding the front seat. Plan with the correct restraint instead. Transportstyrelsen: child rules |  |  | Official recommendations. Trafikverket recommends rear-facing travel until at least four to five years, preferably longer. Transportstyrelsen's advice says as long as possible, normally around four. These are recommendations, not a single legal birthday on which to turn the seat. Choose equipment that fits the child and car and stays within its approved size and weight limits. Reaching 135 cm does not automatically produce good adult-belt fit. Trafikverket: children in cars · Transportstyrelsen: child protection |  |  |  | Never place a rear-facing child restraint in front of an active passenger airbag. Trafikverket advises at least 140 cm in front of an active airbag unless the manufacturer recommends otherwise; Transportstyrelsen gives more conservative advice for children in restraints. Resolve seating and airbag compatibility using the vehicle and restraint instructions before travelling. An airbag supplements a belt; it does not replace one. Adjust the head restraint for the person occupying the seat. Children in cars · Airbags · Seats and head restraints |  |  |  | How protection works |  | Technical explanation · Head restraints. In a rear impact, the seat and torso can move while the head lags behind. A correctly designed and adjusted head restraint helps limit damaging head movement relative to the torso and reduce neck-injury risk. Trafikverket advises positioning the top at the crown of the head and keeping the gap behind the head as small as possible. Adjust it for the occupant before driving; a comfort setting is not the same as a protective setting. A head restraint cannot guarantee that injury will be avoided. Trafikverket: seats and head restraints |  |  | Why children face backwards. A young child's head is relatively heavy and the neck is vulnerable. In a frontal collision, a rear-facing seat supports the head and body together, takes up collision forces and distributes the load across the supported body. The neck does not have to restrain the heavy head on its own in the same way as when facing forwards. This is why the recommendations above concern protection, not only seat orientation. Follow the seat's size limits, fitting instructions and airbag compatibility. Trafikverket: child head and neck protection · Transportstyrelsen: rear-facing collision protection |  |  |  | Controlled deformation. Crumple zones are parts of a vehicle designed to deform progressively in a collision, absorbing energy while the passenger compartment's structure protects the occupants' space. Spreading the deceleration over a longer time reduces forces acting on the people inside. A car remaining visually undamaged is not the objective: designed deformation can be part of its protection. Belts and suitable child restraints still matter, and no structure makes every collision survivable. Western Australia government: structure and crumple zones |  |  | Practice example. A family prepares a car for a child and an adult passenger. They check rear-facing seat fit and airbag compatibility, and adjust the adult's head restraint. After discussing crash protection, they recognise that the restraint, seat and deforming vehicle structure have different roles that work together. | Apply the learning | An adult and child stand beside an open rear door. The empty booster and rear bench face forwards. This scene does not demonstrate installation or belt fit; follow the child-restraint and vehicle instructions. |  | An adult and child stand beside an open rear door. The empty booster and rear bench face forwards. This scene does not demonstrate installation or belt fit; follow the child-restraint and vehicle instructions. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked decision. A child reaches the legal height threshold, but the belt still lies badly. The adult checks an appropriate approved booster rather than treating the threshold as an instruction to discard it. |  |  | Knowledge check. (1) Is a rear-facing seat safe in front of an active airbag for a short trip? (2) What does a head restraint do? (3) Why does rear-facing travel protect a small child? (4) Why are crumple zones designed to deform? | Show answer |  | Remember: Legal minimums, official recommendations and equipment compatibility answer different questions. | Sources | Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §1 | Seat-belt rules | Så skyddar du barnen – regler och tips | Barn i bil | Airbags | Säten och huvudstöd | New or used vehicle buyers | Previous: A check before moving | Next: Move with control

Trafikverket advises positioning the top at the crown of the head and keeping the gap behind the head as small as possible. cases.subject: M02-L03/crumple-zones
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 2. Prepare a car that is ready | Protect everyone inside |  | Your goal: Select suitable restraints for passengers and explain how belts, headrests and airbags work together. |  | Requirements. In an ordinary car journey, occupants must use an available belt-equipped place and wear the belt. Children under 135 cm normally need an appropriate child restraint. The driver must take appropriate measures to ensure passengers under 15 use the required protection. Limited exceptions exist, including specified short occasional journeys, and should not become a routine travel plan. Seat-belt rules · Traffic Regulation, chapter 4 §§10–10d |  |  |  | For a child aged three or more but shorter than 135 cm, an occasional short transport without an available child restraint is an exception only under the stated conditions: use the belt where possible and not the front seat of a passenger car or light goods vehicle. For a child under three, the exception is an occasional short taxi trip, also excluding the front seat. Plan with the correct restraint instead. Transportstyrelsen: child rules |  |  | Official recommendations. Trafikverket recommends rear-facing travel until at least four to five years, preferably longer. Transportstyrelsen's advice says as long as possible, normally around four. These are recommendations, not a single legal birthday on which to turn the seat. Choose equipment that fits the child and car and stays within its approved size and weight limits. Reaching 135 cm does not automatically produce good adult-belt fit. Trafikverket: children in cars · Transportstyrelsen: child protection |  |  |  | Never place a rear-facing child restraint in front of an active passenger airbag. Trafikverket advises at least 140 cm in front of an active airbag unless the manufacturer recommends otherwise; Transportstyrelsen gives more conservative advice for children in restraints. Resolve seating and airbag compatibility using the vehicle and restraint instructions before travelling. An airbag supplements a belt; it does not replace one. Adjust the head restraint for the person occupying the seat. Children in cars · Airbags · Seats and head restraints |  |  |  | How protection works |  | Technical explanation · Head restraints. In a rear impact, the seat and torso can move while the head lags behind. A correctly designed and adjusted head restraint helps limit damaging head movement relative to the torso and reduce neck-injury risk. Trafikverket advises positioning the top at the crown of the head and keeping the gap behind the head as small as possible. Adjust it for the occupant before driving; a comfort setting is not the same as a protective setting. A head restraint cannot guarantee that injury will be avoided. Trafikverket: seats and head restraints |  |  | Why children face backwards. A young child's head is relatively heavy and the neck is vulnerable. In a frontal collision, a rear-facing seat supports the head and body together, takes up collision forces and distributes the load across the supported body. The neck does not have to restrain the heavy head on its own in the same way as when facing forwards. This is why the recommendations above concern protection, not only seat orientation. Follow the seat's size limits, fitting instructions and airbag compatibility. Trafikverket: child head and neck protection · Transportstyrelsen: rear-facing collision protection |  |  |  | Controlled deformation. Crumple zones are parts of a vehicle designed to deform progressively in a collision, absorbing energy while the passenger compartment's structure protects the occupants' space. Spreading the deceleration over a longer time reduces forces acting on the people inside. A car remaining visually undamaged is not the objective: designed deformation can be part of its protection. Belts and suitable child restraints still matter, and no structure makes every collision survivable. Western Australia government: structure and crumple zones |  |  | Practice example. Choose equipment that fits the child and car and stays within its approved size and weight limits. Reaching 135 cm does not automatically produce good adult-belt fit. Trafikverket: children in cars · Transportstyrelsen: child protection |  |  |  | Never place a rear-facing child restraint in front of an active passenger airbag. Trafikverket advises at least 140 cm in front of an active airbag unless the manufacturer recommends otherwise; Transportstyrelsen gives more conservative advice for children in restraints. Resolve seating and airbag compatibility using the vehicle and restraint instructions before travelling. An airbag supplements a belt; it does not replace one. Adjust the head restraint for the person occupying the seat. Children in cars · Airbags · Seats and head restraints |  |  |  | How protection works |  | Technical explanation · Head restraints. In a rear impact, the seat and torso can move while the head lags behind. A correctly designed and adjusted head restraint helps limit damaging head movement relative to the torso and reduce neck-injury risk. Trafikverket advises positioning the top at the crown of the head and keeping the gap behind the head as small as possible. Adjust it for the occupant before driving; a comfort setting is not the same as a protective setting. A head restraint cannot guarantee that injury will be avoided. Trafikverket: seats and head restraints |  |  | Why children face backwards. A young child's head is relatively heavy and the neck is vulnerable. In a frontal collision, a rear-facing seat supports the head and body together, takes up collision forces and distributes the load across the supported body. The neck does not have to restrain the heavy head on its own in the same way as when facing forwards. This is why the recommendations above concern protection, not only seat orientation. Follow the seat's size limits, fitting instructions and airbag compatibility. Trafikverket: child head and neck protection · Transportstyrelsen: rear-facing collision protection |  |  |  | Controlled deformation. Crumple zones are parts of a vehicle designed to deform progressively in a collision, absorbing energy while the passenger compartment's structure protects the occupants' space. Spreading the deceleration over a longer time reduces forces acting on the people inside. A car remaining visually undamaged is not the objective: designed deformation can be part of its protection. Belts and suitable child restraints still matter, and no structure makes every collision survivable. Western Australia government: structure and crumple zones |  |  | Practice example. A family prepares a car for a child and an adult passenger. They check rear-facing seat fit and airbag compatibility, and adjust the adult's head restraint. After discussing crash protection, they recognise that the restraint, seat and deforming vehicle structure have different roles that work together. | Apply the learning | An adult and child stand beside an open rear door. The empty booster and rear bench face forwards. This scene does not demonstrate installation or belt fit; follow the child-restraint and vehicle instructions. |  | An adult and child stand beside an open rear door. The empty booster and rear bench face forwards. This scene does not demonstrate installation or belt fit; follow the child-restraint and vehicle instructions. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked decision. A child reaches the legal height threshold, but the belt still lies badly. The adult checks an appropriate approved booster rather than treating the threshold as an instruction to discard it. |  |  | Knowledge check. (4) Why are crumple zones designed to deform? | Hide answer |  |  | Answer: (1) No. Trip length does not make it safe. cases.subject: M02-L04
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 2. Prepare a car that is ready | Move with control |  | Your goal: Plan observation and control for starting, stopping, reversing, hill starts and turning, and explain why supervised practice is needed. |  | Requirements. Before moving away from the edge, changing position or lane, you must ensure the movement can be made without danger or unnecessary obstruction. Turning around and reversing must be possible without danger or obstruction to other road users. Signal your intention where required, but a signal does not give you priority. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§43, 46 and 65–66 |  |  | Learning approach. Break a manoeuvre into preparation, observation, controlled movement and reassessment. Choose a place with enough room; check around the vehicle and along the intended path; move only while the space remains safe. Stop and reassess when the view changes. Looking once before starting is not continuous observation. |  | A hill start is a control task: prevent unintended movement while coordinating the actual vehicle's transmission, brakes and accelerator. Do not copy pedal sequences between cars without instruction. Reversing, parking and turning also need practical feedback about vehicle dimensions and the path followed by its corners. The official practical test may examine these skills, including effective braking. Practise braking exercises only in suitable, supervised conditions—not as an experiment in ordinary traffic. Trafikverket: manoeuvring and braking |  | The driver is in the left-hand seat and looks around before moving. Controls are illustrative; learn the actual vehicle. |  | The driver is in the left-hand seat and looks around before moving. Controls are illustrative; learn the actual vehicle. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. | Apply the learning | A car and van occupy adjacent bays. A pedestrian is on the footway between the bays and the access lane. Consider what the driver may lose sight of. Diagram not to scale. |  | A car and van occupy adjacent bays. A pedestrian is on the footway between the bays and the access lane. Consider what the driver may lose sight of. Diagram not to scale. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked decision. While reversing into a space, a driver loses sight of a person who was beside the car. The driver stops. The empty camera image is not enough to resolve where the person went; direct observation and an adequate overall view are still needed. |  |  | Knowledge check. If you have signalled and started moving, must another road user always make room? | Show answer |  | Remember: Slow control gives you opportunities to observe and stop; it does not remove the need to look. | Sources | Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §1 | Trafikverket: safety check | Previous: Protect everyone inside | Next: Review and self-assessment

cases.subject: M03-L01
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 3. Read the road before acting | Recognise what a sign asks |  | Your goal: Classify the main sign families and describe the decision each one prompts. |  | Start with purpose, then read the specific symbol and any supplementary panel. The official catalogue groups signs by function. Do not rely on colour alone: similar shapes can communicate different duties, and some important signs have distinctive shapes. Transportstyrelsen: sign catalogue |  |  | Five sign families Separate examples, not a roadside assembly. Read each caption as well as the shape and colour. | Children ahead. Two children inside a warning triangle. | Enlarge Children ahead image |  | Children often cross or remain near this stretch. The sign supplies a warning, not a numerical speed limit. Two children inside a warning triangle. | Give way. Inverted triangular give-way sign. | Enlarge Give way image |  | Yield to vehicles on the crossing road or route. With a distance or stop-ahead panel, this can instead be advance information. Inverted triangular give-way sign. |  | Continue the learning | Maximum speed. Red-bordered yellow circle displaying 30: maximum 30 km/h. | Enlarge Maximum speed image |  | Do not exceed the displayed speed in km/h. A junction alone does not necessarily end the limit, and conditions may require a lower speed. Red-bordered yellow circle displaying 30: maximum 30 km/h. | Mandatory direction. Arrow points left. | Enlarge Mandatory direction image |  | Travel only in a direction shown by the arrow or arrows. Arrow points left. | Built-up area. Black settlement skyline on white. | Enlarge Built-up area image |  | A built-up area begins. Establish the applicable speed limit and other rules; a separate sign may prescribe a different limit. Black settlement skyline on white. |  | Continue the learning |  |  | Family |  | A — warning |  | What to establish |  | The nature of a hazard ahead |  | A useful driving question |  | What might be hidden, and how much space do I need? |  |  | Family |  | B — priority |  | What to establish |  | A duty or relationship at a conflict point |  | A useful driving question |  | Must I yield or stop, and to whom? |  |  | Family |  | C — prohibition/restriction |  | What to establish |  | What movement, vehicle or limit is restricted |  | A useful driving question |  | Does this apply to my vehicle and journey? |  |  | Family |  | D — mandatory instruction |  | What to establish |  | The required route, side or permitted traffic |  | A useful driving question |  | Which path must I take? |  |  | Family |  | E — instruction |  | What to establish |  | A road or area with a particular meaning or regime |  | A useful driving question |  | Which rules begin or end here?

cases.subject: M03-L02
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 3. Read the road before acting | Combine the instructions |  | Your goal: Interpret signs, panels, markings and signals together, including authorised directions. |  | Requirements. Follow the traffic instructions that apply to you. Where an instruction differs from a general traffic rule, the instruction governs. A steady traffic-light indication takes precedence over a yield or stop sign; a police officer's direction takes precedence over the rules and ordinary traffic instructions. This is not a rule that a green signal cancels every other restriction. Authorised guards also give traffic directions that must be followed. Traffic Regulation, chapter 2 §§2–4 |  |  | Authorised directions Separate examples. A static picture does not show the complete movement; read the description and the official instruction. | Police stop instruction — front and rear. Officer faces the viewer with one arm extended sideways. | Enlarge Police stop instruction — front and rear image |  | Traffic approaching the officer from the front or rear must stop; traffic approaching from the sides may proceed. The officer's continuing orientation matters even after the arm movement. Officer faces the viewer with one arm extended sideways. |  | Continue the learning | Police stop instruction — palm facing you. Officer raises a palm towards approaching traffic. | Enlarge Police stop instruction — palm facing you image |  | Stop if the officer's palm faces you. A stop paddle may be used instead. Officer raises a palm towards approaching traffic. | Traffic guard — stop. Guard faces approaching traffic and holds a red flag sideways. | Enlarge Traffic guard — stop image |  | Stop if the guard faces you. A red lamp is used in darkness; an authorised stop sign marked Vakt may also be used. Guard faces approaching traffic and holds a red flag sideways. | Traffic guard identifier. Garment identification panel bearing VAKT. | Enlarge Traffic guard identifier image |  | The guard identifier must be worn on the front and back. It identifies the role rather than giving a separate movement instruction. Garment identification panel bearing VAKT. |  | For ordinary vehicle signals: red means stop; red and amber together still mean stop, with green approaching. Green permits movement, subject to other duties and space ahead. Amber means stop unless, when green changes to amber, you are already so close that stopping would be dangerous. Flashing amber requires particular caution; read the signs and applicable rules. Arrow signals apply to the direction indicated. Road Signs Regulation, chapter 3 §§3–6 |  |  | Ordinary vehicle signals Red, red/amber, green and amber appear in that order. Flashing amber is a separate condition, not the next stage of the normal cycle. Arrow indications apply to the direction shown. | Red vehicle signal. Red left arrow, red full lamp and red bicycle signal examples. | Enlarge Red vehicle signal image |  | Stop before the stop line or, if none, before the signal. An outline arrow limits the indication to the direction shown. Red left arrow, red full lamp and red bicycle signal examples. | Red and amber vehicle signal. Red and amber illuminated together in arrow, full-lamp and bicycle examples. | Enlarge Red and amber vehicle signal image |  | Green is about to follow, but the stop instruction still applies. Do not start merely because amber has appeared. Red and amber illuminated together in arrow, full-lamp and bicycle examples.

cases.subject: M03-L03
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 3. Read the road before acting | Find your way without rushing |  | Your goal: Use direction, facility and service signs to prepare route choices early. |  | Direction information appears before and at decision points. An advance direction sign helps you understand a junction or exit before reaching it; lane direction information helps you select a suitable lane. Direction signs for walking and cycling serve those modes and should not be mistaken for a car route. Facility, service and tourism signs help locate destinations; they do not cancel restrictions on access. Road Signs Regulation, chapter 2, F/G/H/I families |  |  | Advance directions and lane choice Sample destinations are independent examples. For the three-second following-distance guideline, select a fixed roadside point, such as a pole or sign. When the rear of the vehicle ahead passes it, start counting at a steady seconds pace. Stop when the front of your car reaches the same point. Arriving before three seconds indicates a short gap against that guideline: ease back smoothly and check again. You count “one thousand and one, one thousand and two, one thousand and three”. If your car reaches the sign while you are still on “two”, increase the gap smoothly. At a hypothetical constant 60 km/h, three seconds represents 60 ÷ 3.6 × 3 = 50 metres. A timed gap therefore represents more metres at higher speed, without requiring you to estimate metres by eye. |  | Margins and braking distance |  | Safety advice · When someone follows too closely. Increase your gap to the vehicle ahead gradually, allowing you to ease off and brake more gently if traffic slows. This gives the following driver more time to respond. Do not brake sharply to warn or punish them, or accelerate into an unsafe speed. If an emergency requires braking, brake as necessary; this advice does not mean withholding it. With the same effective grip and braking deceleration on the same gradient, braking distance is approximately proportional to speed squared: 2 × speed → 4 × braking distance. In a constant-deceleration model, distance = speed² ÷ (2 × deceleration), with speed in metres per second. Doubling speed multiplies the numerator by four. Real conditions and brake response can change; this is a comparison under stated assumptions. Trafikverket: VGU braking-distance equation |  |  | Hypothetical comparison. Assume a level road, unchanged vehicle/load/grip, constant braking deceleration of 5 m/s² and a one-second response delay. At 40 km/h, braking distance is about 12.3 m and reaction distance 11.1 m. At 80 km/h they are 49.4 m and 22.2 m: braking quadruples while reaction distance doubles. Total stopping distances are about 23.5 m and 71.6 m, so the total does not quadruple. These invented model conditions explain the relationship; they are not predicted stopping distances for your car. |  | A rough calculation method |  | Approximate exercise model · Keep the methods separate. Define v as speed in km/h and t as the supplied reaction time in seconds. Exact constant-speed reaction distance is (v ÷ 3.6) × t metres; braking is not included. When an exercise specifies the rough method below, use both rough estimates together rather than substituting an exact reaction value. |  | Rough reaction estimate: R = (v ÷ 10) × t × 3 metres. Divide speed by ten, multiply by the supplied seconds, then by three. Trafiko: approximate stopping method documents the one-second shortcut; multiplication by a supplied t is editorial proportional arithmetic. Half a second gives half the one-second estimate; two seconds gives twice it. These are supplied exercise inputs, not claims about every driver's reaction time. |  |  | Rough braking estimate: B = (v ÷ 10)² × 0.4 metres. Divide speed by ten, square that result, then multiply by 0.4. Trafiko: approximate stopping method describes this shortcut under good-brake, good-tyre and dry-asphalt assumptions. White diagonal lines on a dark background. |  | Think of stopping in two parts. During the time between noticing a hazard and beginning effective braking, the vehicle still travels. After that, it travels while slowing. More speed consumes more distance during the same delay and increases the energy that must be removed. Less available friction reduces what the tyres can do for braking and steering. Trafikverket: speed and impact · VTI friction report, sections 4.2–4.3 |  |  |  | Continue the learning |  | Illustrative calculation, not a stopping-distance prediction. A speed of 50 km/h is approximately 13.9 metres per second: 50 ÷ 3.6. If a hypothetical response delay is one second, that is about 14 metres before braking begins. At 80 km/h the same assumed delay consumes about 22 metres. These figures are unit conversions using an assumed delay; people do not all react in one second, and braking distance has not yet been added. |  | Learning approach. Scan far enough ahead to see developing situations, while revisiting the near area, mirrors and places where someone may enter. Avoid staring at one hazard until everything else disappears from attention. Increase your margin when information is poor. A timed following-gap check can help you notice a short gap, but no fixed number is safe in every condition. |  | Safety advice · Check a timed gap. For the three-second following-distance guideline, select a fixed roadside point, such as a pole or sign. When the rear of the vehicle ahead passes it, start counting at a steady seconds pace. Stop when the front of your car reaches the same point. Arriving before three seconds indicates a short gap against that guideline: ease back smoothly and check again. Three seconds is a guideline, not a statutory fixed interval or a guarantee; poor grip, visibility or other hazards require more space and an appropriate speed. Keep observing the road while counting. NSW Government: fixed-point following-gap method |  |  | Fixed-point example. The car ahead passes a sign. You count “one thousand and one, one thousand and two, one thousand and three”. If your car reaches the sign while you are still on “two”, increase the gap smoothly. At a hypothetical constant 60 km/h, three seconds represents 60 ÷ 3.6 × 3 = 50 metres. A timed gap therefore represents more metres at higher speed, without requiring you to estimate metres by eye. |  | Margins and braking distance |  | Safety advice · When someone follows too closely. Increase your gap to the vehicle ahead gradually, allowing you to ease off and brake more gently if traffic slows. This gives the following driver more time to respond. Do not brake sharply to warn or punish them, or accelerate into an unsafe speed. If an emergency requires braking, brake as necessary; this advice does not mean withholding it. Northern Ireland government: tailgater response |  |  | Tailgater example. Maya has a close follower and sees brake lights farther ahead. She eases off early to create room in front and slows progressively. She cannot control the follower, but she can reduce the need for a sudden stop. |  | Physical explanation · Twice the speed. With the same effective grip and braking deceleration on the same gradient, braking distance is approximately proportional to speed squared: 2 × speed → 4 × braking distance. In a constant-deceleration model, distance = speed² ÷ (2 × deceleration), with speed in metres per second. Doubling speed multiplies the numerator by four. Real conditions and brake response can change; this is a comparison under stated assumptions. Trafikverket: VGU braking-distance equation |  |  | Hypothetical comparison. Assume a level road, unchanged vehicle/load/grip, constant braking deceleration of 5 m/s² and a one-second response delay. At 40 km/h, braking distance is about 12.3 m and reaction distance 11.1 m. At 80 km/h they are 49.4 m and 22.2 m: braking quadruples while reaction distance doubles. Total stopping distances are about 23.5 m and 71.6 m, so the total does not quadruple. These invented model conditions explain the relationship; they are not predicted stopping distances for your car. |  | A rough calculation method |  | Approximate exercise model · Keep the methods separate. Define v as speed in km/h and t as the supplied reaction time in seconds. Exact constant-speed reaction distance is (v ÷ 3.6) × t metres; braking is not included. When an exercise specifies the rough method below, use both rough estimates together rather than substituting an exact reaction value. |  | Rough reaction estimate: R = (v ÷ 10) × t × 3 metres. Divide speed by ten, multiply by the supplied seconds, then by three. Trafiko: approximate stopping method documents the one-second shortcut; multiplication by a supplied t is editorial proportional arithmetic. Half a second gives half the one-second estimate; two seconds gives twice it. These are supplied exercise inputs, not claims about every driver's reaction time. |  |  | Rough braking estimate: B = (v ÷ 10)² × 0.4 metres. Divide speed by ten, square that result, then multiply by 0.4. Trafiko: approximate stopping method describes this shortcut under good-brake, good-tyre and dry-asphalt assumptions. The coefficient is an exercise assumption, not a universal result for a real car or road. Supplied reaction time does not change the braking part in this model. |  |  | Rough total: S = R + B. Calculate both parts separately with metres, then add. Keep decimal precision during the working; round only the final result if a precision is requested. These shortcuts teach arithmetic, not a safe-distance guarantee or a prediction for an actual hazard. |  | Source and assumption limits. Trafiko is a commercial teaching source, cited only for these approximate shortcuts. Trafikverket: stopping-distance principles supports reaction plus braking and dependence on speed and conditions, but does not supply these constants. Its illustrated distances have different assumptions and must not be mixed with this model. Real stopping depends on grip, gradient, tyres, brakes, response and other conditions. Retain the exact conversion and separate constant-deceleration comparison above under their own assumptions. |  |  | Apply the rough model |  | Worked approximate examples · Calculate both parts. Use the rough exercise equations consistently; each reaction time below is a supplied hypothetical input. |  | Example A · 40 km/h and 0.5 seconds. First v ÷ 10 = 4. Reaction R = 4 × 0.5 × 3 = 6 m. Braking B = 4² × 0.4 = 6.4 m. Total S = 6 + 6.4 = 12.4 m. The half-second input affects reaction, not braking. |  | Example B · 70 km/h and one second. First v ÷ 10 = 7. Reaction R = 7 × 1 × 3 = 21 m. Braking B = 7² × 0.4 = 19.6 m. Total S = 21 + 19.6 = 40.6 m. Squaring seven gives 49; do not multiply speed itself by 0.4. |  | Example C · 50 km/h and two seconds. First v ÷ 10 = 5. Reaction R = 5 × 2 × 3 = 30 m. Braking B = 5² × 0.4 = 10 m. Total S = 30 + 10 = 40 m. Doubling reaction time doubles this model's reaction estimate, leaving braking unchanged. |  | Compare separately with exact conversion. At 50 km/h and two seconds, exact constant-speed reaction distance is (50 ÷ 3.6) × 2 = about 27.8 m, compared with the shortcut's 30 m. Dividing the shortcut factor 0.3 by the exact conversion factor 1 ÷ 3.6 gives 1.08: an 8% overestimate for reaction distance. Mixing 27.8 m with rough braking of 10 m gives about 37.8 m, not the exercise model's 40 m. Keep exact conversion separate from the rough-model answer. |  | Try the approximate process. Calculate reaction, braking and total for (A) 30 km/h and 0.5 seconds, (B) 80 km/h and one second, and (C) 100 km/h and two seconds. Give each part in metres, check the square, then add. Answers are in the separate lesson answer section. |  | Apply the learning | A driver approaches a queue on a divided road. The illustrated gap is not a measured safe following distance. Look ahead and leave room to respond. |  | A driver approaches a queue on a divided road. The illustrated gap is not a measured safe following distance. Look ahead and leave room to respond. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked decision. You can see over the roof of the car ahead that traffic is slowing. Ease your approach early rather than waiting for its brake lights at a short distance. The benefit is having choices before braking becomes urgent. |  |  | Knowledge check. (1) If response delay doubles at the same speed, what happens to reaction distance? (2) How do you time a three-second following gap? (3) Why increase the forward gap when someone follows too closely? (4) With unchanged braking deceleration, how does doubled speed affect braking distance, and does total stopping distance also quadruple? (5) Complete the three approximate exercises above and explain why you should keep exact reaction conversion separate. | Show answer |  | Remember: Space is useful because it gives you time to notice, decide and act. | Sources | Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §1 | VTI friction report, section 4.3 | Taxi Driver Manual | Safe stopping distance | KRAV Grundvärden, Vägar och gators utformning (VGU) | Stoppsträcka, reaktionssträcka & bromssträcka | Hastighet och stoppsträcka | Hastighet och krockvåld - www.trafikverket.se | Previous: Find your way without rushing | Next: Review and self-assessment
