cases.text: |  |  | End of recommended maximum speed. White diagonal lines on a dark background. | Enlarge End of recommended maximum speed image |  | The temporary speed recommendation ends. White diagonal lines on a dark background. |  | Think of stopping in two parts. During the time between noticing a hazard and beginning effective braking, the vehicle still travels. After that, it travels while slowing. More speed consumes more distance during the same delay and increases the energy that must be removed. Less available friction reduces what the tyres can do for braking and steering. Trafikverket: speed and impact · VTI friction report, sections 4.2–4.3 |  |  |  | Continue the learning |  | Illustrative calculation, not a stopping-distance prediction. A speed of 50 km/h is approximately 13.9 metres per second: 50 ÷ 3.6. If a hypothetical response delay is one second, that is about 14 metres before braking begins. At 80 km/h the same assumed delay consumes about 22 metres. These figures are unit conversions using an assumed delay; people do not all react in one second, and braking distance has not yet been added. |  | Learning approach. Scan far enough ahead to see developing situations, while revisiting the near area, mirrors and places where someone may enter. Avoid staring at one hazard until everything else disappears from attention. Increase your margin when information is poor. A timed following-gap check can help you notice a short gap, but no fixed number is safe in every condition. |  | Safety advice · Check a timed gap. For the three-second following-distance guideline, select a fixed roadside point, such as a pole or sign. When the rear of the vehicle ahead passes it, start counting at a steady seconds pace. Stop when the front of your car reaches the same point. Arriving before three seconds indicates a short gap against that guideline: ease back smoothly and check again. Three seconds is a guideline, not a statutory fixed interval or a guarantee; poor grip, visibility or other hazards require more space and an appropriate speed. Keep observing the road while counting. NSW Government: fixed-point following-gap method |  |  | Fixed-point example. The car ahead passes a sign. You count “one thousand and one, one thousand and two, one thousand and three”. If your car reaches the sign while you are still on “two”, increase the gap smoothly. At a hypothetical constant 60 km/h, three seconds represents 60 ÷ 3.6 × 3 = 50 metres. A timed gap therefore represents more metres at higher speed, without requiring you to estimate metres by eye. |  | Margins and braking distance |  | Safety advice · When someone follows too closely. Increase your gap to the vehicle ahead gradually, allowing you to ease off and brake more gently if traffic slows. This gives the following driver more time to respond. Do not brake sharply to warn or punish them, or accelerate into an unsafe speed. If an emergency requires braking, brake as necessary; this advice does not mean withholding it. Northern Ireland government: tailgater response |  |  | Tailgater example. Maya has a close follower and sees brake lights farther ahead. She eases off early to create room in front and slows progressively. She cannot control the follower, but she can reduce the need for a sudden stop. |  | Physical explanation · Twice the speed. With the same effective grip and braking deceleration on the same gradient, braking distance is approximately proportional to speed squared: 2 × speed → 4 × braking distance. In a constant-deceleration model, distance = speed² ÷ (2 × deceleration), with speed in metres per second. Doubling speed multiplies the numerator by four. Real conditions and brake response can change; this is a comparison under stated assumptions. Trafikverket: VGU braking-distance equation |  |  | Hypothetical comparison. Assume a level road, unchanged vehicle/load/grip, constant braking deceleration of 5 m/s² and a one-second response delay. At 40 km/h, braking distance is about 12.3 m and reaction distance 11.1 m. At 80 km/h they are 49.4 m and 22.2 m: braking quadruples while reaction distance doubles. Total stopping distances are about 23.5 m and 71.6 m, so the total does not quadruple. These invented model conditions explain the relationship; they are not predicted stopping distances for your car. |  | A rough calculation method |  | Approximate exercise model · Keep the methods separate. Define v as speed in km/h and t as the supplied reaction time in seconds. Exact constant-speed reaction distance is (v ÷ 3.6) × t metres; braking is not included. When an exercise specifies the rough method below, use both rough estimates together rather than substituting an exact reaction value. |  | Rough reaction estimate: R = (v ÷ 10) × t × 3 metres. Divide speed by ten, multiply by the supplied seconds, then by three. Trafiko: approximate stopping method documents the one-second shortcut; multiplication by a supplied t is editorial proportional arithmetic. Half a second gives half the one-second estimate; two seconds gives twice it. These are supplied exercise inputs, not claims about every driver's reaction time. |  |  | Rough braking estimate: B = (v ÷ 10)² × 0.4 metres. Divide speed by ten, square that result, then multiply by 0.4. Trafiko: approximate stopping method describes this shortcut under good-brake, good-tyre and dry-asphalt assumptions. The coefficient is an exercise assumption, not a universal result for a real car or road. Supplied reaction time does not change the braking part in this model. |  |  | Rough total: S = R + B. Calculate both parts separately with metres, then add. Keep decimal precision during the working; round only the final result if a precision is requested. These shortcuts teach arithmetic, not a safe-distance guarantee or a prediction for an actual hazard. |  | Source and assumption limits. Trafiko is a commercial teaching source, cited only for these approximate shortcuts. Trafikverket: stopping-distance principles supports reaction plus braking and dependence on speed and conditions, but does not supply these constants. Its illustrated distances have different assumptions and must not be mixed with this model. Real stopping depends on grip, gradient, tyres, brakes, response and other conditions. Retain the exact conversion and separate constant-deceleration comparison above under their own assumptions. |  |  | Apply the rough model |  | Worked approximate examples · Calculate both parts. Use the rough exercise equations consistently; each reaction time below is a supplied hypothetical input. |  | Example A · 40 km/h and 0.5 seconds. First v ÷ 10 = 4. Reaction R = 4 × 0.5 × 3 = 6 m. Look ahead and leave room to respond. |  | A driver approaches a queue on a divided road. The illustrated gap is not a measured safe following distance. Look ahead and leave room to respond. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked decision. You can see over the roof of the car ahead that traffic is slowing. After that, it travels while slowing. More speed consumes more distance during the same delay and increases the energy that must be removed. Less available friction reduces what the tyres can do for braking and steering. A speed of 50 km/h is approximately 13.9 metres per second: 50 ÷ 3.6. If a hypothetical response delay is one second, that is about 14 metres before braking begins. At 80 km/h the same assumed delay consumes about 22 metres. These figures are unit conversions using an assumed delay; people do not all react in one second, and braking distance has not yet been added. |  | Learning approach. Scan far enough ahead to see developing situations, while revisiting the near area, mirrors and places where someone may enter. Avoid staring at one hazard until everything else disappears from attention. Increase your margin when information is poor. A timed following-gap check can help you notice a short gap, but no fixed number is safe in every condition. |  | Safety advice · Check a timed gap. For the three-second following-distance guideline, select a fixed roadside point, such as a pole or sign. When the rear of the vehicle ahead passes it, start counting at a steady seconds pace. Stop when the front of your car reaches the same point. Arriving before three seconds indicates a short gap against that guideline: ease back smoothly and check again. Three seconds is a guideline, not a statutory fixed interval or a guarantee; poor grip, visibility or other hazards require more space and an appropriate speed. Keep observing the road while counting. NSW Government: fixed-point following-gap method |  |  | Fixed-point example. The car ahead passes a sign. Avoid staring at one hazard until everything else disappears from attention. Increase your margin when information is poor. A timed following-gap check can help you notice a short gap, but no fixed number is safe in every condition. |  | Safety advice · Check a timed gap. Keep observing the road while counting. NSW Government: fixed-point following-gap method |  |  | Fixed-point example. The car ahead passes a sign. At a hypothetical constant 60 km/h, three seconds represents 60 ÷ 3.6 × 3 = 50 metres. She eases off early to create room in front and slows progressively. She cannot control the follower, but she can reduce the need for a sudden stop. |  | Physical explanation · Twice the speed. Look ahead and leave room to respond. |  | A driver approaches a queue on a divided road. The illustrated gap is not a measured safe following distance. Look ahead and leave room to respond. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked decision. You can see over the roof of the car ahead that traffic is slowing. cases.subject: M03-L04/production-0010
cases.text: |  |  | End of recommended maximum speed. White diagonal lines on a dark background. | Enlarge End of recommended maximum speed image |  | The temporary speed recommendation ends. White diagonal lines on a dark background. |  | Think of stopping in two parts. During the time between noticing a hazard and beginning effective braking, the vehicle still travels. After that, it travels while slowing. More speed consumes more distance during the same delay and increases the energy that must be removed. Less available friction reduces what the tyres can do for braking and steering. Trafikverket: speed and impact · VTI friction report, sections 4.2–4.3 |  |  |  | Continue the learning |  | Illustrative calculation, not a stopping-distance prediction. A speed of 50 km/h is approximately 13.9 metres per second: 50 ÷ 3.6. If a hypothetical response delay is one second, that is about 14 metres before braking begins. At 80 km/h the same assumed delay consumes about 22 metres. These figures are unit conversions using an assumed delay; people do not all react in one second, and braking distance has not yet been added. |  | Learning approach. Scan far enough ahead to see developing situations, while revisiting the near area, mirrors and places where someone may enter. Avoid staring at one hazard until everything else disappears from attention. Increase your margin when information is poor. A timed following-gap check can help you notice a short gap, but no fixed number is safe in every condition. |  | Safety advice · Check a timed gap. For the three-second following-distance guideline, select a fixed roadside point, such as a pole or sign. When the rear of the vehicle ahead passes it, start counting at a steady seconds pace. Stop when the front of your car reaches the same point. Arriving before three seconds indicates a short gap against that guideline: ease back smoothly and check again. Three seconds is a guideline, not a statutory fixed interval or a guarantee; poor grip, visibility or other hazards require more space and an appropriate speed. Keep observing the road while counting. NSW Government: fixed-point following-gap method |  |  | Fixed-point example. The car ahead passes a sign. You count “one thousand and one, one thousand and two, one thousand and three”. If your car reaches the sign while you are still on “two”, increase the gap smoothly. At a hypothetical constant 60 km/h, three seconds represents 60 ÷ 3.6 × 3 = 50 metres. A timed gap therefore represents more metres at higher speed, without requiring you to estimate metres by eye. |  | Margins and braking distance |  | Safety advice · When someone follows too closely. Increase your gap to the vehicle ahead gradually, allowing you to ease off and brake more gently if traffic slows. This gives the following driver more time to respond. Do not brake sharply to warn or punish them, or accelerate into an unsafe speed. If an emergency requires braking, brake as necessary; this advice does not mean withholding it. Northern Ireland government: tailgater response |  |  | Tailgater example. Maya has a close follower and sees brake lights farther ahead. She eases off early to create room in front and slows progressively. She cannot control the follower, but she can reduce the need for a sudden stop. |  | Physical explanation · Twice the speed. With the same effective grip and braking deceleration on the same gradient, braking distance is approximately proportional to speed squared: 2 × speed → 4 × braking distance. In a constant-deceleration model, distance = speed² ÷ (2 × deceleration), with speed in metres per second. Doubling speed multiplies the numerator by four. Real conditions and brake response can change; this is a comparison under stated assumptions. Trafikverket: VGU braking-distance equation |  |  | Hypothetical comparison. Assume a level road, unchanged vehicle/load/grip, constant braking deceleration of 5 m/s² and a one-second response delay. At 40 km/h, braking distance is about 12.3 m and reaction distance 11.1 m. At 80 km/h they are 49.4 m and 22.2 m: braking quadruples while reaction distance doubles. Total stopping distances are about 23.5 m and 71.6 m, so the total does not quadruple. These invented model conditions explain the relationship; they are not predicted stopping distances for your car. |  | A rough calculation method |  | Approximate exercise model · Keep the methods separate. Define v as speed in km/h and t as the supplied reaction time in seconds. Exact constant-speed reaction distance is (v ÷ 3.6) × t metres; braking is not included. When an exercise specifies the rough method below, use both rough estimates together rather than substituting an exact reaction value. |  | Rough reaction estimate: R = (v ÷ 10) × t × 3 metres. Divide speed by ten, multiply by the supplied seconds, then by three. Trafiko: approximate stopping method documents the one-second shortcut; multiplication by a supplied t is editorial proportional arithmetic. Half a second gives half the one-second estimate; two seconds gives twice it. These are supplied exercise inputs, not claims about every driver's reaction time. |  |  | Rough braking estimate: B = (v ÷ 10)² × 0.4 metres. Divide speed by ten, square that result, then multiply by 0.4. Trafiko: approximate stopping method describes this shortcut under good-brake, good-tyre and dry-asphalt assumptions. The coefficient is an exercise assumption, not a universal result for a real car or road. Supplied reaction time does not change the braking part in this model. |  |  | Rough total: S = R + B. Calculate both parts separately with metres, then add. Keep decimal precision during the working; round only the final result if a precision is requested. These shortcuts teach arithmetic, not a safe-distance guarantee or a prediction for an actual hazard. |  | Source and assumption limits. Trafiko is a commercial teaching source, cited only for these approximate shortcuts. Trafikverket: stopping-distance principles supports reaction plus braking and dependence on speed and conditions, but does not supply these constants. Its illustrated distances have different assumptions and must not be mixed with this model. Real stopping depends on grip, gradient, tyres, brakes, response and other conditions. Retain the exact conversion and separate constant-deceleration comparison above under their own assumptions. |  |  | Apply the rough model |  | Worked approximate examples · Calculate both parts. Use the rough exercise equations consistently; each reaction time below is a supplied hypothetical input. |  | Example A · 40 km/h and 0.5 seconds. First v ÷ 10 = 4. Reaction R = 4 × 0.5 × 3 = 6 m. Braking B = 4² × 0.4 = 6.4 m. Total S = 6 + 6.4 = 12.4 m. The half-second input affects reaction, not braking. |  | Example B · 70 km/h and one second. First v ÷ 10 = 7. Reaction R = 7 × 1 × 3 = 21 m. Braking B = 7² × 0.4 = 19.6 m. Total S = 21 + 19.6 = 40.6 m. Squaring seven gives 49; do not multiply speed itself by 0.4. |  | Example C · 50 km/h and two seconds. First v ÷ 10 = 5. Reaction R = 5 × 2 × 3 = 30 m. Braking B = 5² × 0.4 = 10 m. Total S = 30 + 10 = 40 m. Doubling reaction time doubles this model's reaction estimate, leaving braking unchanged. |  | Compare separately with exact conversion. At 50 km/h and two seconds, exact constant-speed reaction distance is (50 ÷ 3.6) × 2 = about 27.8 m, compared with the shortcut's 30 m. Dividing the shortcut factor 0.3 by the exact conversion factor 1 ÷ 3.6 gives 1.08: an 8% overestimate for reaction distance. Mixing 27.8 m with rough braking of 10 m gives about 37.8 m, not the exercise model's 40 m. Keep exact conversion separate from the rough-model answer. |  | Try the approximate process. Calculate reaction, braking and total for (A) 30 km/h and 0.5 seconds, (B) 80 km/h and one second, and (C) 100 km/h and two seconds. Give each part in metres, check the square, then add. Answers are in the separate lesson answer section. |  | Apply the learning | A driver approaches a queue on a divided road. The illustrated gap is not a measured safe following distance. Look ahead and leave room to respond. |  | A driver approaches a queue on a divided road. The illustrated gap is not a measured safe following distance. Look ahead and leave room to respond. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked decision. You can see over the roof of the car ahead that traffic is slowing. Ease your approach early rather than waiting for its brake lights at a short distance. The benefit is having choices before braking becomes urgent. |  |  | Knowledge check. (1) If response delay doubles at the same speed, what happens to reaction distance? (2) How do you time a three-second following gap? (3) Why increase the forward gap when someone follows too closely? (4) With unchanged braking deceleration, how does doubled speed affect braking distance, and does total stopping distance also quadruple? (5) Complete the three approximate exercises above and explain why you should keep exact reaction conversion separate. | Show answer |  | Remember: Space is useful because it gives you time to notice, decide and act. | Sources | Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §1 | VTI friction report, section 4.3 | Taxi Driver Manual | Safe stopping distance | KRAV Grundvärden, Vägar och gators utformning (VGU) | Stoppsträcka, reaktionssträcka & bromssträcka | Hastighet och stoppsträcka | Hastighet och krockvåld - www.trafikverket.se | Previous: Find your way without rushing | Next: Review and self-assessment

First v ÷ 10 = 5. Reaction R = 5 × 2 × 3 = 30 m. Braking B = 5² × 0.4 = 10 m. Total S = 30 + 10 = 40 m. Doubling reaction time doubles this model's reaction estimate, leaving braking unchanged. |  | Compare separately with exact conversion. At 50 km/h and two seconds, exact constant-speed reaction distance is (50 ÷ 3.6) × 2 = about 27.8 m, compared with the shortcut's 30 m. Dividing the shortcut factor 0.3 by the exact conversion factor 1 ÷ 3.6 gives 1.08: an 8% overestimate for reaction distance. Mixing 27.8 m with rough braking of 10 m gives about 37.8 m, not the exercise model's 40 m. Keep exact conversion separate from the rough-model answer. |  | Try the approximate process. Calculate reaction, braking and total for (A) 30 km/h and 0.5 seconds, (B) 80 km/h and one second, and (C) 100 km/h and two seconds. Give each part in metres, check the square, then add. Answers are in the separate lesson answer section. |  | Apply the learning | A driver approaches a queue on a divided road. The illustrated gap is not a measured safe following distance. Look ahead and leave room to respond. |  | A driver approaches a queue on a divided road. The illustrated gap is not a measured safe following distance. Look ahead and leave room to respond. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked decision. You can see over the roof of the car ahead that traffic is slowing. Ease your approach early rather than waiting for its brake lights at a short distance. The benefit is having choices before braking becomes urgent. |  |  | Knowledge check. (1) If response delay doubles at the same speed, what happens to reaction distance? (2) How do you time a three-second following gap? (3) Why increase the forward gap when someone follows too closely? (4) With unchanged braking deceleration, how does doubled speed affect braking distance, and does total stopping distance also quadruple? (5) Complete the three approximate exercises above and explain why you should keep exact reaction conversion separate. | Show answer |  | Remember: Space is useful because it gives you time to notice, decide and act. | Sources | Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §1 | VTI friction report, section 4.3 | Taxi Driver Manual | Safe stopping distance | KRAV Grundvärden, Vägar och gators utformning (VGU) | Stoppsträcka, reaktionssträcka & bromssträcka | Hastighet och stoppsträcka | Hastighet och krockvåld - www.trafikverket.se | Previous: Find your way without rushing | Next: Review and self-assessment

cases.subject: M04-L02
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 4. Negotiate shared space | Turn with a complete picture |  | Your goal: Plan observation, signalling, position and margins for turns and lane changes. |  | Requirements. Before a turn, check that it will not obstruct oncoming traffic or traffic on the road you are entering. Pay attention to people travelling in the same direction, including those behind you. Position early: normally the right-hand lane for a right turn and the left-hand lane for a left turn where multiple approach lanes exist, subject to applicable signs, markings and space provisions. On a two-way road, a left turn is normally prepared near the road centre; on a one-way carriageway, near the left edge. When stopped waiting to turn left across oncoming traffic, keep your front wheels pointing straight ahead. Your indicator communicates the intended turn; your wheels do not need to point along that intended route while you wait. If a vehicle hits you from behind, front wheels already turned left can direct the pushed car into oncoming traffic. Keeping them straight helps reduce that risk, but cannot guarantee protection in a collision. Begin steering into the turn only when there is a safe opportunity to make it. New York DMV: waiting to turn left |  |  | Waiting is different from turning. Follow the positioning, signalling and observation requirements above. The wheel-position advice does not create permission to enter or block a junction, ignore a signal, or obstruct someone else's path. Continue observing oncoming traffic, the receiving road, crossings and vehicles behind you while waiting. Recheck the full path before moving. |  | Practice example. Sami is stopped in a suitable position, signalling left while oncoming cars pass. A passenger suggests turning the wheels left now to be ready. Sami keeps them straight: preparing the intention is different from starting the movement. Once the gap and receiving road permit a safe turn, he moves and steers into it. Examples of straight, branching and turning lane arrows. |  | For a lane change or significant sideways movement, signal clearly and in time, then check that the movement can be made without danger or unnecessary obstruction. The indicator announces an intention, not a claim on a gap. Drivers who notice another vehicle intending to join their lane must adjust speed to help; when two lanes merge into one, both drivers must adapt with mutual consideration. These duties work together. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§43–44 and 65–66 |  |  | Changing and merging lanes Compare merging, lane increase, lane reduction and a lane-change arrow. Establish the actual road layout before deciding how to move. | Merge. Two paths combine into one upward arrow. | Enlarge Merge image |  | Two lanes or carriageways join. Drivers must adapt with mutual consideration; this is not an instruction to force a gap. Two paths combine into one upward arrow. | Additional lane. An additional lane opens on the left. | Enlarge Additional lane image |  | The number of lanes increases. Read the diagram for direction and any physical separation. An additional lane opens on the left. | Lane reduction. The left-hand lane merges into the remaining forward lane. | Enlarge Lane reduction image |  | The number of lanes decreases. Use the diagram to plan a safe change early. The left-hand lane merges into the remaining forward lane. |  | Continue the learning | Change-lane arrow. White change-lane arrow bending sideways. | Enlarge Change-lane arrow image |  | A lane change is needed promptly. Check that the manoeuvre can be made safely. White change-lane arrow bending sideways. |  | Learning approach. Read the path through the turn, not just the point at which you steer. Check the mirror view and the areas it does not cover. Look for a cyclist alongside before turning across their route. Recheck the receiving road, crossings and queue space. If the information changes, pause the manoeuvre rather than completing the original plan automatically. |  | Wait before steering |  | Safety advice · Wait with front wheels straight. When stopped waiting to turn left across oncoming traffic, keep your front wheels pointing straight ahead. Your indicator communicates the intended turn; your wheels do not need to point along that intended route while you wait. If a vehicle hits you from behind, front wheels already turned left can direct the pushed car into oncoming traffic. Keeping them straight helps reduce that risk, but cannot guarantee protection in a collision. Begin steering into the turn only when there is a safe opportunity to make it. New York DMV: waiting to turn left |  |  | Waiting is different from turning. Follow the positioning, signalling and observation requirements above. The wheel-position advice does not create permission to enter or block a junction, ignore a signal, or obstruct someone else's path. Continue observing oncoming traffic, the receiving road, crossings and vehicles behind you while waiting. Recheck the full path before moving. |  | Practice example. Sami is stopped in a suitable position, signalling left while oncoming cars pass. A passenger suggests turning the wheels left now to be ready. Sami keeps them straight: preparing the intention is different from starting the movement. Once the gap and receiving road permit a safe turn, he moves and steers into it. On rural roads, use M06-L01 to assess bends, crests and other risks before choosing a turning opportunity. |  |  | Changing lane or merging? | Lane change: two marked lanes continue. A signal communicates an intention; check for a safe opportunity before moving sideways. |  | Lane change: two marked lanes continue. A signal communicates an intention; check for a safe opportunity before moving sideways. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork.

cases.text: |  |  |  | Learning approach. Read the path through the turn, not just the point at which you steer. Check the mirror view and the areas it does not cover. Look for a cyclist alongside before turning across their route. Recheck the receiving road, crossings and queue space. If the information changes, pause the manoeuvre rather than completing the original plan automatically. |  | Wait before steering |  | Safety advice · Wait with front wheels straight. When stopped waiting to turn left across oncoming traffic, keep your front wheels pointing straight ahead. Your indicator communicates the intended turn; your wheels do not need to point along that intended route while you wait. If a vehicle hits you from behind, front wheels already turned left can direct the pushed car into oncoming traffic. Keeping them straight helps reduce that risk, but cannot guarantee protection in a collision. Begin steering into the turn only when there is a safe opportunity to make it. New York DMV: waiting to turn left |  |  | Waiting is different from turning. Follow the positioning, signalling and observation requirements above. The wheel-position advice does not create permission to enter or block a junction, ignore a signal, or obstruct someone else's path. Continue observing oncoming traffic, the receiving road, crossings and vehicles behind you while waiting. Recheck the full path before moving. |  | Practice example. Sami is stopped in a suitable position, signalling left while oncoming cars pass. A passenger suggests turning the wheels left now to be ready. Sami keeps them straight: preparing the intention is different from starting the movement. Once the gap and receiving road permit a safe turn, he moves and steers into it. cases.subject: M04-L04
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 4. Negotiate shared space | Choose a safe path through a roundabout |  | Your goal: Describe an approach, entry and exit plan that accounts for priority, lanes, signalling and nearby crossings. |  | Requirements. Travel anticlockwise and yield on entry to vehicles already circulating. Choose an appropriate lane for the onward route and obey signs and markings. There is no general requirement to signal solely for entering; signal lane changes and significant sideways movements, and signal right when leaving. Any lane change must be safe and must not create unnecessary obstruction. Transportstyrelsen: roundabout guide · Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§13, 22, 43 and 65–66 |  |  |  | Roundabout instructions Approach warning, circulation direction, yielding, lane guidance and island marker are distinct instructions. Read the actual combination on the road. | Roundabout ahead. Circulating arrows inside a warning triangle. | Enlarge Roundabout ahead image |  | Prepare for a roundabout and identify the entry instructions before reaching it. Circulating arrows inside a warning triangle. |  | Continue the learning | Roundabout. Three white arrows circulate anticlockwise on blue. | Enlarge Roundabout image |  | Follow the roundabout circulation. Identify the yielding instruction at the entry separately. Three white arrows circulate anticlockwise on blue. | Give way. Inverted triangular give-way sign. | Enlarge Give way image |  | Yield to vehicles on the crossing road or route. With a distance or stop-ahead panel, this can instead be advance information. Inverted triangular give-way sign. | Roundabout lane arrow. Lane arrow with a roundabout diagram and several onward directions. | Enlarge Roundabout lane arrow image |  | On the approach to a roundabout, this marking helps you choose a suitable lane for the next junction and your onward route. Its layout is adapted to the location. Lane arrow with a roundabout diagram and several onward directions. | Roundabout centre marker. A horizontal blue board bears successive white arrows pointing right. | Enlarge Roundabout centre marker image |  | This identifies the centre around which vehicles circulate in the roundabout. A horizontal blue board bears successive white arrows pointing right. |  | Continue the learning |  | Learning approach. Read the layout before reaching the yield point. Reduce speed enough to judge circulating traffic and the available space. Observe crossings on the approach as separate conflicts. Inside, hold your intended path and continue checking nearby vehicles. A large vehicle may need more room than its apparent lane width suggests. Roundabout guide |  |  | Plan the exit early. Moving from an inner lane across an outer lane is a lane change, even though you call the whole movement “leaving the roundabout.” Do not assume a vehicle beside you will leave at the same exit. If the exit cannot be taken safely, continue as the layout allows and re-plan. On leaving, check the crossing area again; the duties in M04-L03 still apply. Roundabout guide · Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§60–62 |  |  |  |  | Entry and circulation are separate decisions | Give way. Inverted triangular give-way sign. | Roundabout. Three white arrows circulate anticlockwise on blue. | Approach: B1 and D3 identify the entry instructions. The teal car approaches the yield point while the yellow car circulates anticlockwise. |  | Approach: B1 and D3 identify the entry instructions. The teal car approaches the yield point while the yellow car circulates anticlockwise. |  |  | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork.

cases.subject: M05-L01
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 5. Make room in busy streets | See the person behind the movement |  | Your goal: Anticipate the needs of different road users without assuming that everyone sees, hears or moves as you do. |  | Requirements. Show particular consideration for children, older people, school patrols and people whose disability or illness is apparent and affects their use of traffic. Reduce speed appropriately near children, stopped passenger transport and other situations with foreseeable risks. Give pedestrians sufficient room and time when meeting or passing them. Traffic Regulation, chapter 2 §1 and chapter 3 §§15 and 58 |  |  | Learning approach. Look for the space a person needs, not only the space they occupy now. A child may be hidden by a parked car. A cyclist may need to move out from an obstruction. A wheelchair user may need a usable kerb transition. You cannot reliably infer someone's hearing, vision or intentions from a quick glance. Allow time and observe their movement rather than demanding a response through the horn. |  | Observe people and possible movement Children, cyclists and riders have different needs. Sensory-impairment panels are separate examples; absence of a sign does not prove absence of risk. | Pedestrians ahead. Adult and child inside a warning triangle. | Enlarge Pedestrians ahead image |  | People often cross, walk on or remain near this stretch of road. Allow for someone entering your path. Adult and child inside a warning triangle. |  | Continue the learning | Children ahead. Two children inside a warning triangle. | Enlarge Children ahead image |  | Children often cross or remain near this stretch. The sign supplies a warning, not a numerical speed limit. Two children inside a warning triangle. | Cyclists and moped riders ahead. Cyclist inside a warning triangle. | Enlarge Cyclists and moped riders ahead image |  | Cyclists or moped riders often cross or enter the road here. Cyclist inside a warning triangle. |  | Sensory-impairment panels | People with impaired vision. Five black dots arranged horizontally on yellow. | Enlarge People with impaired vision image |  | People with impaired vision commonly use the area. Give them time and space without assuming they have seen you. Five black dots arranged horizontally on yellow. |  | Continue the learning | People with impaired hearing. Three black dots inside a black circle on yellow. | Enlarge People with impaired hearing image |  | People with impaired hearing commonly use the area. Do not assume a horn will be heard. Three black dots inside a black circle on yellow. |  | Horses and riders also belong in your traffic assessment. Vehicle rules apply to riding and leading horses in relevant respects; they are not simply pedestrians because they travel slowly. Give them an unhurried, spacious interaction, and avoid unnecessary noise. This is a cautious application of the general duty of care, not a fixed passing-distance rule. Transportstyrelsen: horses in traffic |  |  | Horses and riders This warning supports early observation. It does not specify a fixed passing distance. | Horse riders ahead. Horse and rider inside a warning triangle. | Enlarge Horse riders ahead image |  | Riders often cross or use this stretch of road. Prepare for an unhurried, spacious encounter. Horse and rider inside a warning triangle.

cases.subject: M05-L02
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 5. Make room in busy streets | When the street changes purpose |  | Your goal: Distinguish ordinary streets from pedestrian streets, walking-speed areas and cycle streets. |  | Requirements. On a pedestrian street (gågata) and in a walking-speed area (gångfartsområde), drive no faster than walking pace and yield to pedestrians. The general rule prohibits parking; a specifically signed lawful parking arrangement must be assessed on its own terms. Walking pace is a condition to match, not a universal speedometer number. Special streets · Traffic Regulation, chapter 8 §1 and chapter 10 §1 |  |  |  | Pedestrian streets and walking-speed areas Two matched start/end pairs. Pedestrian-street access limits differ from walking-speed-area rules. Pedestrian street | Pedestrian street. Adult and child within a blue rectangular sign. | Enlarge Pedestrian street image |  | Special pedestrian-street rules apply, including walking pace and yielding to pedestrians. Motor access is restricted to the permitted purposes; it is not a general shortcut. Adult and child within a blue rectangular sign. |  | Continue the learning | End of pedestrian street. Pedestrian-street symbol crossed by a red diagonal. | Enlarge End of pedestrian street image |  | The pedestrian street ends. Reassess the rules before entering another road. Pedestrian-street symbol crossed by a red diagonal. |  | Walking-speed area | Walking-speed area. Street scene with pedestrians, a car, houses and a playing child. | Enlarge Walking-speed area image |  | Drive at walking pace and yield to pedestrians. Parking is generally prohibited except where a lawful signed arrangement provides otherwise. Street scene with pedestrians, a car, houses and a playing child. | End of walking-speed area. Walking-speed street scene crossed by a red diagonal. | Enlarge End of walking-speed area image |  | The walking-speed area ends. Leaving it does not give you priority over the road you enter. Walking-speed street scene crossed by a red diagonal. |  | Continue the learning |  | Motor vehicles may use a pedestrian street only to cross it, apart from the specified necessary journeys: goods to or from shops or equivalent premises; goods or residents to or from addresses there; guests to or from hotels or equivalent premises; and sick people or people with mobility impairments to or from an address. A convenient shortcut does not qualify. Check additional signs and local restrictions. Traffic Regulation, chapter 8 §1 |  |  | On a cycle street (cykelgata), the maximum is 30 km/h, and motor vehicles must adapt speed to bicycle traffic. Vehicles entering from another road yield to vehicles already on it. Parking is restricted to specially provided places. When leaving a cycle street for another road, the exit yielding rule applies. Special streets · Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §21 and chapter 8 §1a |  |  |  | Cycle streets Matched beginning and ending signs. Retain the entry and exit yielding duties in the lesson. | Cycle street. Bicycle with a smaller car above it on blue. | Enlarge Cycle street image |  | The maximum is 30 km/h and motor vehicles must adapt to bicycle traffic. Apply the cycle-street entry, exit and parking rules too. Bicycle with a smaller car above it on blue. | End of cycle street. Cycle-street bicycle and car crossed by a red diagonal. | Enlarge End of cycle street image |  | The cycle street ends. Apply the yielding rule when leaving it for another road. Cycle-street bicycle and car crossed by a red diagonal.

cases.subject: M05-L03
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 5. Make room in busy streets | Choose a lawful place to stop |  | Your goal: Distinguish stopping from parking and interpret the rules, signs and time panels for a proposed place. |  | Parking is leaving a vehicle stationary for a reason other than traffic conditions, avoiding danger, boarding or alighting, or loading or unloading goods. Remaining behind the wheel does not automatically make waiting “stopping.” Nor does switching on hazard lights create permission. Transportstyrelsen: stopping and parking |  |  | Stopping or parking restrictions Compare no parking with no stopping and parking. An extent marking needs its actual accompanying restriction; it does not create permission. | No parking. Single red diagonal across a blue circle. | Enlarge No parking image |  | Parking is prohibited on the signed side for the applicable extent. This does not make stopping lawful where another rule prohibits it. Single red diagonal across a blue circle. | No stopping or parking. Red cross on a blue circle. | Enlarge No stopping or parking image |  | Both stopping and parking are prohibited for the indicated extent. Waiting with the engine running is not a general exemption. Red cross on a blue circle. |  | Continue the learning | No stopping or parking edge marking. Continuous yellow line at the road edge. | Enlarge No stopping or parking edge marking image |  | The continuous yellow edge marking indicates a stopping and parking prohibition. Continuous yellow line at the road edge. | No parking edge marking. Broken yellow line at the road edge. | Enlarge No parking edge marking image |  | The broken yellow edge marking indicates a parking prohibition; it can also show the extent of a bus stop. Broken yellow line at the road edge. | Reinforcement of a stopping or parking restriction. Yellow zigzag marking reinforcing a stopping or parking restriction. | Enlarge Reinforcement of a stopping or parking restriction image |  | This yellow marking reinforces the applicable M21 or M22 restriction. Identify which prohibition applies. Yellow zigzag marking reinforcing a stopping or parking restriction. |  |  |  | Core requirements. Do not stop or park where you create danger, unnecessarily obstruct traffic or hide a sign or signal. cases.subject: M06-L01
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 6. Travel beyond the town | Read the rural road |  | Your goal: Identify risks from bends, crests, narrow roads, animals and slow vehicles and justify speed and position changes. |  | Requirements. Keep right when meeting another vehicle and leave a safe lateral gap. If an obstruction on your side prevents a safe meeting, stop if necessary to let the approaching vehicle pass. Your speed must suit the visible road and foreseeable hazards, with particular care at bends, crests and narrow meetings. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§14–15 and 30 |  |  | Learning approach. Read the road in sections: the visible straight, the entry to a bend, the portion hidden behind a crest and the next place someone might join. Never extend the clear section in your imagination. A vehicle emerging from a field or a cyclist beyond a bend changes what seemed to be an empty road. |  | Read the rural road ahead Independent examples of bends, gradients, narrowings, uneven road and passing places. Gradient numbers are percentages, not a safe-speed formula. Bends and gradients | Dangerous bend. Left bend. | Enlarge Dangerous bend image |  | A hazardous bend lies ahead. The symbol shows its direction; adjust speed before entering it. Left bend. |  | Continue the learning | Dangerous bend. Right bend. | Enlarge Dangerous bend image |  | A hazardous bend lies ahead. The symbol shows its direction; adjust speed before entering it. Right bend. | Series of dangerous bends. Series of bends, first to the left. | Enlarge Series of dangerous bends image |  | Several hazardous bends lie ahead. The symbol identifies the direction of the first bend. Series of bends, first to the left. | Series of dangerous bends. Series of bends, first to the right. | Enlarge Series of dangerous bends image |  | Several hazardous bends lie ahead. The symbol identifies the direction of the first bend. Series of bends, first to the right. |  | Continue the learning | Steep descent. A descending slope labelled 10 percent. | Enlarge Steep descent image |  | Prepare for a steep downhill section. The number is the gradient in percent, not a speed limit. A descending slope labelled 10 percent. | Steep ascent. An ascending slope labelled 10 percent. | Enlarge Steep ascent image |  | Prepare for a steep uphill section. Read the percentage as a gradient. An ascending slope labelled 10 percent.

cases.subject: M06-L02
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 6. Travel beyond the town | Is passing worth the risk? |  | Your goal: Compare waiting with overtaking using visibility, speed difference, space and a safe completion path. |  | Requirements. Overtake only without danger and with sufficient clear road. Do not start when a following driver has begun overtaking, or pass on the left when the vehicle ahead signals an intended leftward movement. Leave safe lateral clearance and a safe return opportunity. When being overtaken, do not increase speed or otherwise make the pass harder. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§31–38 |  |  | The normal passing side is left. Exceptions include a vehicle turning or clearly preparing to turn left, and the specified rules for marked same-direction lanes on roads limited to 70 km/h or less. Passing in queues or destination lanes has separate provisions; it does not remove the need to protect people at crossings. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§7, 31 and 41–42 |  |  | Restrictions to recognise. Overtaking is generally prohibited immediately before or in a road junction, with specified exceptions for right-side overtaking, police/signal control, or an established yielding/stopping duty on the crossing road. Similar restrictions apply at level crossings, with exceptions for barriers or road-junction-type traffic signals. At an obscured bend or crest, do not use an opposing lane to overtake; the detailed provision contains limited exceptions. Section 39 also contains an exception for passing two-wheeled vehicles without sidecars. That exception does not override the danger prohibition, continuous-line restrictions or the uncontrolled-crossing prohibition. None of these exceptions proves a manoeuvre safe. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §39 |  |  | Do not overtake immediately before or on an uncontrolled pedestrian crossing, uncontrolled cycle passage or cycle crossing. Where parallel-lane passing is legally not classified as overtaking, the special crossing rule still requires a speed allowing an immediate stop for a person on the crossing or passage. Obey signs and continuous-line restrictions as well. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§11, 40–41 |  |  | Overtaking signs and line information The prohibition and its end form a pair. For combined lines, identify the line nearest your lane. M20a warns of a coming centre-line or divider change; it is not an ordinary lane-change arrow. |  | No overtaking. Red and black cars side by side. | Enlarge No overtaking image |  | Do not overtake motor vehicles other than two-wheeled mopeds and motorcycles without sidecars. Other overtaking safety rules still apply; the sign restriction continues to C28. Red and black cars side by side. |  | End of overtaking prohibition. Overtaking symbol crossed by diagonal black lines. | Enlarge End of overtaking prohibition image |  | The prohibition introduced by C27 ends. General overtaking restrictions still apply. Overtaking symbol crossed by diagonal black lines. |  |  | Line information | Warning line. Long white strokes with short gaps. | Enlarge Warning line image |  | Crossing this line is unsuitable because of the traffic conditions. It may also warn of a continuous line ahead. Long white strokes with short gaps. |  | Continue the learning | Continuous line. Single and double continuous white lines. | Enlarge Continuous line image |  | Crossing restrictions apply according to the type of continuous line and the traffic rules. Do not invent an exception merely because the road appears clear. Single and double continuous white lines. | Broken line beside a continuous line. Broken white line beside a continuous line. | Enlarge Broken line beside a continuous line image |  | The continuous line governs a driver on its side of the marking. Do not treat the broken line on the other side as permission to change lanes. Broken white line beside a continuous line. | Warning line beside a continuous line. Warning line beside a continuous line. | Enlarge Warning line beside a continuous line image |  | The continuous-line side restricts lane changes; the warning-line side indicates that crossing is unsuitable. Warning line beside a continuous line.

cases.subject: M06-L04
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 6. Travel beyond the town | Expect an interrupted route |  | Your goal: Interpret railway-crossing and roadworks information and approach changed lanes, queues and barriers safely. |  | Railway requirements. Approach with particular care and at a speed that allows a stop before the crossing. Do not enter when a train or tram is approaching, a red signal shows, an audible warning sounds, a barrier is lowering, lowered or rising, or you might have to stop on the tracks. Cross without unnecessary delay only when it is permitted and there is room beyond. Traffic Regulation, chapter 2 §7 |  |  | Railway warnings and crossing controls Advance warnings, three/two/one countdown markers, crossbucks and active controls have different roles. Countdown boards do not specify fixed metre intervals. A still image does not reproduce flashing or sound. No crossing-ID number is invented. Advance warnings | Rail crossing with barriers. Barrier pictogram inside a warning triangle. | Enlarge Rail crossing with barriers image |  | A railway or tramway crossing fitted with barriers lies ahead. Follow its signals and barrier indications. Barrier pictogram inside a warning triangle. |  | Continue the learning | Rail crossing without barriers. Locomotive inside a warning triangle. | Enlarge Rail crossing without barriers image |  | Prepare for a railway crossing without barriers. The lack of barriers does not mean a train cannot approach. Locomotive inside a warning triangle. | Tram crossing without barriers. Tram inside a warning triangle. | Enlarge Tram crossing without barriers image |  | A tramway crossing without barriers lies ahead. Tram inside a warning triangle. |  | Countdown to the crossing | Rail-crossing countdown. Three red diagonal bars on a yellow board. | Enlarge Rail-crossing countdown image |  | The three markers divide the approach into thirds. They do not represent a universal fixed distance in metres. Three red diagonal bars on a yellow board. |  | Continue the learning | Rail-crossing countdown. Two red diagonal bars on a yellow board. | Enlarge Rail-crossing countdown image |  | The three markers divide the approach into thirds. They do not represent a universal fixed distance in metres. cases.subject: M07-L01
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 7. Adapt when conditions change | Drive within what you can see |  | Your goal: Choose a visibility and lighting strategy for darkness, fog and glare. |  | Requirements. Your speed must allow a stop within the visible road and before foreseeable hazards. Darkness does not create a separate allowance to travel beyond the distance you can assess. Keep the required lamps on; daytime running lights alone may be insufficient when conditions deteriorate. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§14–15 and 68–71 |  |  | Another changing condition: crosswinds Independent crosswind warnings. The windsock shows the wind direction; neither example is a fog warning or a headlight instruction. | Crosswinds. Windsock extends towards the left. | Enlarge Crosswinds image |  | Strong crosswinds commonly occur on this stretch. The symbol is adapted to local conditions. Windsock extends towards the left. | Crosswinds. Windsock extends towards the right. | Enlarge Crosswinds image |  | Strong crosswinds commonly occur on this stretch. The symbol is adapted to local conditions. Windsock extends towards the right. |  | Continue the learning |  | Use main beam when needed for a sufficient field of view, but not where the road is adequately lit, where it can dazzle an approaching driver or an adjacent rail/ship operator, or at close distance behind another vehicle. Dipped beam is the usual driving light. In fog or heavy precipitation, front fog lights may replace dipped beam; the prohibited combinations must not be used together. A rear fog light is restricted to fog, heavy precipitation or comparable reduced visibility and must not dazzle a following driver. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§69–72 |  |  | Learning approach. Make lighting and speed one decision. If you dip the lights and can see less far, reassess speed immediately. Check the edges of the visible road for people and animals rather than assuming a dark area is empty. Keep windows and mirrors clear enough for a useful view and learn demisting controls before a difficult journey. |  | Automatic lighting is an aid, not confirmation that every required lamp is on. In a car whose daytime-light mode leaves the rear lights off, check the actual setting when darkness or bad weather arrives. Transportstyrelsen: vehicle lighting |  |  | Light and visual information |  | Lighting choice · Name the prohibited pair. Do not use dipped headlights and front fog lights together. In fog or heavy precipitation, front fog lights may replace dipped headlights; they are not an extra light to add to them. Select a permitted mode and check it on the actual vehicle. Transportstyrelsen: dipped beam and front fog lights |  |  | Central vision · Read the detail. Central vision supplies the fine detail where you are looking directly. Reading the precise wording on a road sign relies particularly on it. Merely noticing a sign at the edge of your view does not establish what its text says. Official driver-vision guidance |  |  | Peripheral vision · Notice, then inspect. Peripheral or side vision surrounds your direct focus. It can alert you to movement, a developing hazard or a traffic change outside that focus. Move your eyes, and head where needed, to inspect the relevant object directly while maintaining control and awareness of the road. For example, notice movement near the verge, then look to identify whether it is a person about to enter your path. Keep scanning; staring at one sign can leave other information unattended. Official driver-vision guidance |  |  | One light · Keep width uncertain. One approaching light at night does not prove a narrow motorcycle. A wider car can have a failed headlight. Transportstyrelsen documents defective car headlights; the practical inference is to allow for a vehicle whose full width is not yet visible. Preserve a safe lateral margin and adapt speed to the view rather than squeezing past on a guessed width. Transportstyrelsen: defective car headlights |  |  | Reassess the visible road | Rain and darkness shorten the usable view. The teal car travels on the right. Reassess speed and check the actual exterior-light setting; the illustration does not identify a lamp mode or a measured stopping distance. |  | Rain and darkness shorten the usable view. The teal car travels on the right. Reassess speed and check the actual exterior-light setting; the illustration does not identify a lamp mode or a measured stopping distance. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked decision. Rain becomes heavy during a daytime trip. The dashboard remains illuminated, but the driver checks and selects the appropriate exterior lighting rather than inferring that the rear lights must be on. The driver also reduces speed for the shorter usable view. |  | Check your understanding |  |  | Knowledge check. (1) Can you maintain speed solely because the limit is unchanged after dipping main beam? (2) May dipped headlights and front fog lights be used together? (3) Which vision role reads precise sign text, and which can alert you to movement outside direct focus? (4) Does one approaching light prove a narrow motorcycle? | Show answer |  | Remember: Adjust speed to the information the light actually gives you. | Sources | Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §1 | Transportstyrelsen: vehicle lighting | Choose the right vehicle lighting | Vision Impairment and DMV Requirements | Halvljus – vanligaste felet vid besiktning | Previous: Adapt when conditions change | Next: Grip is a changing resource

Adapt when conditions change | Drive within what you can see |  | Your goal: Choose a visibility and lighting strategy for darkness, fog and glare. |  | Requirements. Your speed must allow a stop within the visible road and before foreseeable hazards. Darkness does not create a separate allowance to travel beyond the distance you can assess. Keep the required lamps on; daytime running lights alone may be insufficient when conditions deteriorate. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§14–15 and 68–71 |  |  | Another changing condition: crosswinds Independent crosswind warnings. The windsock shows the wind direction; neither example is a fog warning or a headlight instruction. | Crosswinds. Windsock extends towards the left. | Enlarge Crosswinds image |  | Strong crosswinds commonly occur on this stretch. The symbol is adapted to local conditions. Windsock extends towards the left. | Crosswinds. Windsock extends towards the right. | Enlarge Crosswinds image |  | Strong crosswinds commonly occur on this stretch. The symbol is adapted to local conditions. Windsock extends towards the right. |  | Continue the learning |  | Use main beam when needed for a sufficient field of view, but not where the road is adequately lit, where it can dazzle an approaching driver or an adjacent rail/ship operator, or at close distance behind another vehicle. Dipped beam is the usual driving light. In fog or heavy precipitation, front fog lights may replace dipped beam; the prohibited combinations must not be used together. A rear fog light is restricted to fog, heavy precipitation or comparable reduced visibility and must not dazzle a following driver. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§69–72 |  |  | Learning approach. Make lighting and speed one decision. If you dip the lights and can see less far, reassess speed immediately. Check the edges of the visible road for people and animals rather than assuming a dark area is empty. Keep windows and mirrors clear enough for a useful view and learn demisting controls before a difficult journey. |  | Automatic lighting is an aid, not confirmation that every required lamp is on. In a car whose daytime-light mode leaves the rear lights off, check the actual setting when darkness or bad weather arrives. Transportstyrelsen: vehicle lighting |  |  | Light and visual information |  | Lighting choice · Name the prohibited pair. Do not use dipped headlights and front fog lights together. In fog or heavy precipitation, front fog lights may replace dipped headlights; they are not an extra light to add to them. Select a permitted mode and check it on the actual vehicle. Transportstyrelsen: dipped beam and front fog lights |  |  | Central vision · Read the detail. Central vision supplies the fine detail where you are looking directly. Reading the precise wording on a road sign relies particularly on it. Merely noticing a sign at the edge of your view does not establish what its text says. Official driver-vision guidance |  |  | Peripheral vision · Notice, then inspect. Peripheral or side vision surrounds your direct focus. It can alert you to movement, a developing hazard or a traffic change outside that focus. Move your eyes, and head where needed, to inspect the relevant object directly while maintaining control and awareness of the road. For example, notice movement near the verge, then look to identify whether it is a person about to enter your path. Keep scanning; staring at one sign can leave other information unattended. Official driver-vision guidance |  |  | One light · Keep width uncertain. One approaching light at night does not prove a narrow motorcycle. A wider car can have a failed headlight. Transportstyrelsen documents defective car headlights; the practical inference is to allow for a vehicle whose full width is not yet visible. Preserve a safe lateral margin and adapt speed to the view rather than squeezing past on a guessed width. Transportstyrelsen: defective car headlights |  |  | Reassess the visible road | Rain and darkness shorten the usable view. The teal car travels on the right. Reassess speed and check the actual exterior-light setting; the illustration does not identify a lamp mode or a measured stopping distance. |  | Rain and darkness shorten the usable view. The teal car travels on the right. Reassess speed and check the actual exterior-light setting; the illustration does not identify a lamp mode or a measured stopping distance. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked decision. Rain becomes heavy during a daytime trip. The dashboard remains illuminated, but the driver checks and selects the appropriate exterior lighting rather than inferring that the rear lights must be on. The driver also reduces speed for the shorter usable view. |  | Check your understanding |  |  | Knowledge check. (1) Can you maintain speed solely because the limit is unchanged after dipping main beam? (2) May dipped headlights and front fog lights be used together? (3) Which vision role reads precise sign text, and which can alert you to movement outside direct focus? (4) Does one approaching light prove a narrow motorcycle? | Show answer |  | Remember: Adjust speed to the information the light actually gives you. | Sources | Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §1 | Transportstyrelsen: vehicle lighting | Choose the right vehicle lighting | Vision Impairment and DMV Requirements | Halvljus – vanligaste felet vid besiktning | Previous: Adapt when conditions change | Next: Grip is a changing resource

cases.subject: M07-L02
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 7. Adapt when conditions change | Grip is a changing resource |  | Your goal: Explain how surface conditions, tyres and driver inputs affect stability, steering and braking. |  | Tyres need friction to change the vehicle's speed and direction. Braking while cornering shares that capacity; ABS can help preserve steering forces during braking, but the available friction still limits the result. Water, snow and ice change the conditions at the tyre contact, so dry-road expectations cannot simply be carried into them. VTI friction report, sections 4.2–4.3 |  |  | Warnings about grip Independent slippery-road and loose-chippings warnings. Observe the actual surface; these warnings are not limited to winter. | Slippery road. Skidding car inside a red-bordered yellow triangle. | Enlarge Slippery road image |  | The road may be slippery. Do not assume that the warning refers only to snow or ice. Skidding car inside a red-bordered yellow triangle. | Loose chippings. Car wheel throws stones inside a warning triangle. | Enlarge Loose chippings image |  | There is a risk of stones being thrown up. This warning is not normally used where that risk is routine, such as a gravel road. Car wheel throws stones inside a warning triangle. |  | Continue the learning |  | Requirements for ordinary light cars and their trailers, checked 1 October 2026. Between 1 December and 31 March, winter tyres or equivalent equipment are required when winter conditions exist. Snow, ice, slush or frost on any part of the road counts; police determine conditions at the location. The minimum tread depth for the ordinary light-vehicle case is 3 mm. Studless winter tyres for the car need the mountain/snowflake marking. Winter tyres |  |  | Studded tyres are permitted from 1 October to 15 April and outside that period when winter conditions exist or are expected. Do not mix studded and non-studded tyres on an ordinary passenger car or light goods vehicle. In winter conditions, a studded towing car requires a studded trailer; the reverse combination is allowed. A light-trailer transition permits specified winter-designed M+S tyres through 30 November 2028. Exemptions and heavier-vehicle cases need their own checks; they are not the ordinary car rule. Winter tyres · Traffic Regulation, chapter 4 §§18a–18d |  |  |  | Check local studded-tyre restrictions Seasonal permission to use studs does not override a local prohibition. This road sign is not a tyre sidewall marking. | No studded-tyre motor vehicles except class II mopeds. Studded tyre crossed by a red diagonal. | Enlarge No studded-tyre motor vehicles except class II mopeds image |  | The prohibition concerns motor vehicles with studded tyres. Class II mopeds are included only if a supplementary panel says so. Studded tyre crossed by a red diagonal. |  | For summer conditions, the minimum tread depth is 1.6 mm. Transportstyrelsen recommends placing the tyres with the best grip or greatest tread depth at the rear and checking pressure against the vehicle's instructions. A legal minimum is not a promise of equal performance in every condition. Transportstyrelsen: tyres |  |  | Read changing surfaces |  | Surface change · A bridge can freeze first. A bridge is exposed to cold air above and below. That exposure can cool it faster than neighbouring road supported by ground, so moisture can freeze on the bridge while the approach still appears clear. It is a possibility, not a rule that every bridge always freezes first. Anticipate uncertain grip and reduce speed before reaching the bridge. National Weather Service: bridge cooling |  |  | Rain on a cold road · Ice can hide. Rainwater can freeze when it meets a road surface cold enough for ice to form, producing a thin, nearly invisible slippery layer. The road may look wet, and the air temperature can be above zero while the surface is still below freezing. Near-zero air alone does not prove ice, but it calls for attention to surface conditions, more space and lower speed. Trafikverket: deceptive ice and cold roads |  |  | First rain after dry weather · Residues matter. During a dry spell, dust, dirt and oily residues can accumulate. The first rain can mix with these contaminants and make the road unusually slippery. Reassess speed and separation as rain starts; do not assume a light shower immediately washes the surface clean or that a fixed time restores grip. County Fire: rain after a dry spell |  |  | Worked surface decision. A light shower begins after dry weather as you approach a bridge in near-freezing conditions. Plan for both wet residues and possible local ice. The clear-looking approach does not measure the grip on the bridge. |  | Understand grip and handling |  | Rear stability · Why the best grip belongs at the rear. Transportstyrelsen recommends the best-grip or deepest-tread tyres at the rear to reduce skid risk in braking and bends, for both front- and rear-wheel-drive cars. Better rear grip helps reduce the risk of the rear sliding outward and rotating the car. Suitable tyres and stability assistance still cannot guarantee control. Transportstyrelsen: best tyres at the rear · VTI: rear grip and oversteer |  |  |  | Oversteer · Rear grip loss. In the loss-of-grip situation, the rear tyres lose sufficient lateral grip, the tail swings outward and the car rotates more than intended into the turn. This can develop into a spin. VTI: oversteer and rear stability |  |  | Understeer · Front grip loss. In the loss-of-grip situation, the front tyres cannot supply the lateral grip needed for the requested turn. The car turns less than intended and follows a straighter, wider path; adding more steering does not guarantee the requested curve. These are grip-loss explanations, not a full definition of every vehicle's normal handling characteristics. VTI: handling paths · NHTSA: front-axle grip limit |  |  |  | Aquaplaning · Water interrupts contact. If water builds between tyres and road, it can support the tyre on a film and reduce or remove effective tyre-road contact. Steering and braking then have less grip to work with. Reduce speed before standing water and uncertain wet surfaces. PennDOT: aquaplaning |  |  | Response · Ease off smoothly. If aquaplaning starts and there is space to slow gradually, ease off the accelerator, keep steering steady and avoid abrupt steering or hard braking. Make only gentle necessary corrections as contact returns. This is different from M02-L01's ABS emergency-stop instruction: ABS cannot create grip where a tyre is separated from the road by water. An immediate collision emergency needs action appropriate to the actual situation; this advice does not establish a universal ban on braking. Near-zero air alone does not prove ice, but it calls for attention to surface conditions, more space and lower speed. The first rain can mix with these contaminants and make the road unusually slippery. Reassess speed and separation as rain starts; do not assume a light shower immediately washes the surface clean or that a fixed time restores grip. Plan for both wet residues and possible local ice. The clear-looking approach does not measure the grip on the bridge. |  | Understand grip and handling |  | Rear stability · Why the best grip belongs at the rear. Transportstyrelsen recommends the best-grip or deepest-tread tyres at the rear to reduce skid risk in braking and bends, for both front- and rear-wheel-drive cars. Better rear grip helps reduce the risk of the rear sliding outward and rotating the car. Suitable tyres and stability assistance still cannot guarantee control. Transportstyrelsen: best tyres at the rear · VTI: rear grip and oversteer |  |  |  | Oversteer · Rear grip loss. In the loss-of-grip situation, the rear tyres lose sufficient lateral grip, the tail swings outward and the car rotates more than intended into the turn. This can develop into a spin. An immediate collision emergency needs action appropriate to the actual situation; this advice does not establish a universal ban on braking. A light, unresponsive steering feel over standing water raises a different possibility: aquaplaning. Recognise the mechanism, preserve margins and practise vehicle-specific emergency handling only with suitable instruction. |  | Prepare before grip changes |  | Learning approach. Reduce speed and increase space before reaching uncertain grip. Avoid demanding abrupt braking, steering and acceleration together. Do not experiment with skid recovery in ordinary traffic. Establish the actual vehicle's emergency-braking behaviour through appropriate instruction and risk training. Studded tyre crossed by a red diagonal. | Enlarge No studded-tyre motor vehicles except class II mopeds image |  | The prohibition concerns motor vehicles with studded tyres. Class II mopeds are included only if a supplementary panel says so. Studded tyre crossed by a red diagonal. |  | For summer conditions, the minimum tread depth is 1.6 mm. Transportstyrelsen recommends placing the tyres with the best grip or greatest tread depth at the rear and checking pressure against the vehicle's instructions. A legal minimum is not a promise of equal performance in every condition. Transportstyrelsen: tyres |  |  | Read changing surfaces |  | Surface change · A bridge can freeze first. A bridge is exposed to cold air above and below. That exposure can cool it faster than neighbouring road supported by ground, so moisture can freeze on the bridge while the approach still appears clear. It is a possibility, not a rule that every bridge always freezes first. Anticipate uncertain grip and reduce speed before reaching the bridge. National Weather Service: bridge cooling |  |  | Rain on a cold road · Ice can hide. Rainwater can freeze when it meets a road surface cold enough for ice to form, producing a thin, nearly invisible slippery layer. The road may look wet, and the air temperature can be above zero while the surface is still below freezing. Near-zero air alone does not prove ice, but it calls for attention to surface conditions, more space and lower speed. Trafikverket: deceptive ice and cold roads |  |  | First rain after dry weather · Residues matter. During a dry spell, dust, dirt and oily residues can accumulate. The first rain can mix with these contaminants and make the road unusually slippery. Reassess speed and separation as rain starts; do not assume a light shower immediately washes the surface clean or that a fixed time restores grip. County Fire: rain after a dry spell |  |  | Worked surface decision. A light shower begins after dry weather as you approach a bridge in near-freezing conditions. Plan for both wet residues and possible local ice. The clear-looking approach does not measure the grip on the bridge. |  | Understand grip and handling |  | Rear stability · Why the best grip belongs at the rear. Transportstyrelsen recommends the best-grip or deepest-tread tyres at the rear to reduce skid risk in braking and bends, for both front- and rear-wheel-drive cars. Better rear grip helps reduce the risk of the rear sliding outward and rotating the car. Suitable tyres and stability assistance still cannot guarantee control. Transportstyrelsen: best tyres at the rear · VTI: rear grip and oversteer |  |  |  | Oversteer · Rear grip loss. In the loss-of-grip situation, the rear tyres lose sufficient lateral grip, the tail swings outward and the car rotates more than intended into the turn. This can develop into a spin. VTI: oversteer and rear stability |  |  | Understeer · Front grip loss. In the loss-of-grip situation, the front tyres cannot supply the lateral grip needed for the requested turn. The car turns less than intended and follows a straighter, wider path; adding more steering does not guarantee the requested curve. These are grip-loss explanations, not a full definition of every vehicle's normal handling characteristics. VTI: handling paths · NHTSA: front-axle grip limit |  |  |  | Aquaplaning · Water interrupts contact. If water builds between tyres and road, it can support the tyre on a film and reduce or remove effective tyre-road contact. Steering and braking then have less grip to work with. Reduce speed before standing water and uncertain wet surfaces. PennDOT: aquaplaning |  |  | Response · Ease off smoothly. If aquaplaning starts and there is space to slow gradually, ease off the accelerator, keep steering steady and avoid abrupt steering or hard braking. Make only gentle necessary corrections as contact returns. This is different from M02-L01's ABS emergency-stop instruction: ABS cannot create grip where a tyre is separated from the road by water. An immediate collision emergency needs action appropriate to the actual situation; this advice does not establish a universal ban on braking. PennDOT: aquaplaning response |  |  |  | Worked grip comparison. A rear slide swinging the tail outward is oversteer; a front slide that prevents the intended curve is understeer. A light, unresponsive steering feel over standing water raises a different possibility: aquaplaning. Recognise the mechanism, preserve margins and practise vehicle-specific emergency handling only with suitable instruction. |  | Prepare before grip changes |  | Learning approach. Reduce speed and increase space before reaching uncertain grip. Avoid demanding abrupt braking, steering and acceleration together. Do not experiment with skid recovery in ordinary traffic. Establish the actual vehicle's emergency-braking behaviour through appropriate instruction and risk training. Trafikverket: winter driving advice · Risk training |  |  | A dry-looking foreground leads towards a shaded winter bend. The surface appearance is a reason to reassess, not a measurement of friction. No skid-recovery technique or guaranteed tyre performance is shown. |  | A dry-looking foreground leads towards a shaded winter bend. The surface appearance is a reason to reassess, not a measurement of friction. No skid-recovery technique or guaranteed tyre performance is shown. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked decision. Your car has suitable winter tyres, but the next bend is partly shaded and looks different from the road behind. You reduce speed before the bend and preserve margin. Equipment does not establish the grip at that particular point. |  | Check your understanding |  |  | Knowledge check. (1) Does legal tread depth guarantee dry-road spacing on ice? (2) Why can a bridge freeze first? (3) What can rain form on a sufficiently cold road? (4) Why can first rain after dry weather be unusually slippery? (5) Why place the best-grip tyres at the rear? (6) Compare oversteer and understeer in a grip-loss situation. (7) What is aquaplaning, and how should you respond when there is room to slow gradually? | Show answer |  | Remember: Tyres and assistance systems support a cautious plan; they do not create unlimited grip. | Sources | Risk training | Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §1 | VTI friction report, section 4.3 | Winter Driving — Bridges Freeze First | På glid? Nej! Transportstyrelsen recommends placing the tyres with the best grip or greatest tread depth at the rear and checking pressure against the vehicle's instructions. A legal minimum is not a promise of equal performance in every condition. Transportstyrelsen: tyres |  |  | Read changing surfaces |  | Surface change · A bridge can freeze first. A bridge is exposed to cold air above and below. That exposure can cool it faster than neighbouring road supported by ground, so moisture can freeze on the bridge while the approach still appears clear. It is a possibility, not a rule that every bridge always freezes first. Anticipate uncertain grip and reduce speed before reaching the bridge. Rainwater can freeze when it meets a road surface cold enough for ice to form, producing a thin, nearly invisible slippery layer. The road may look wet, and the air temperature can be above zero while the surface is still below freezing. Near-zero air alone does not prove ice, but it calls for attention to surface conditions, more space and lower speed.
