cases.subject: M07-L03
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 7. Adapt when conditions change | Protect your attention |  | Your goal: Recognise distraction, stress and fatigue and choose an interruption or alternative travel plan. |  | Requirements. During road travel, a driver may use communication equipment only if it does not adversely affect driving. Holding the equipment in the hand while using it is prohibited. Hands-free use is therefore not automatically acceptable: the effect on driving still matters. You must also not drive when exhaustion or another condition prevents safe control. Transportstyrelsen: communication equipment · Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §1 and chapter 4 §10e |  |  |  | Learning approach. Prepare navigation before setting off, place the phone away from casual handling and agree when passengers can help. If a conversation, screen task or emotional reaction is consuming the attention needed for the road, end it. A safe place to stop is the place to resolve a complicated route or urgent message. |  | Attention link. Use M07-L01's notice-then-inspect distinction when scanning. A conversation that consumes attention can delay recognising what peripheral vision has alerted you to. |  |  | Treat fatigue as a reason to change the journey. Plan rest opportunities and stop safely when concentration cannot be maintained. Do not wait for a dramatic event to prove that you are too tired. Trafikverket recommends setting out rested, allowing time and taking breaks on longer journeys. No universal break interval in this material certifies that you can continue safely. Journey advice |  |  | Plan a safe rest stop A rest-area destination can support journey planning. The sign gives no prescribed break interval or assurance that a tired driver can safely continue. | Rest area. Picnic table and tree. | Enlarge Rest area image |  | This identifies a rest area with a toilet accessible to people with mobility impairments. Picnic table and tree. |  | Protect attention before moving | A left-hand-seat driver is parked in a parking area, with the phone in a holder. This is a stopped discussion, not permission to use a screen or conduct a distracting call while driving. cases.subject: M07-L04
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 7. Adapt when conditions change | Change the plan when risk grows |  | Your goal: Reassess a trip when weather, darkness, delays or passenger pressure accumulate. |  | Learning approach. At a meaningful change—worsening visibility, an unexpected closure, a missed rest opportunity—review the whole plan. Ask what has changed in the driver, vehicle, route and time available. A manageable single difficulty may become demanding when several occur together. This is a planning exercise, not a formula that assigns a numerical risk score. |  | Choose between continuing with a suitable margin, stopping safely, changing route, changing driver if lawful and suitable, or cancelling the journey. The choice depends on the actual conditions. A driver unable to maintain safe control must not continue merely because the destination is close. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§1 and 14 |  |  | The syllabus treats route choice, timing, passengers, fatigue and personal motives as parts of driving competence. Use the same questions after a journey: Which warning did I notice early? Which did I explain away because I wanted to finish? Syllabus, chapters 4–5 |  |  | Reconsider the whole journey | Two adults reconsider a journey indoors while rain falls outside and the car remains parked. Use the available route information to choose a realistic alternative before setting off. |  | Two adults reconsider a journey indoors while rain falls outside and the car remains parked. Use the available route information to choose a realistic alternative before setting off. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked decision. A late appointment leaves a driver facing an unfamiliar route in darkness and worsening weather. Instead of protecting the original arrival time, the driver finds a safe stopping place, tells the person waiting and chooses a realistic alternative. The change happens while there is still time to make it calmly. |  | Check your understanding |  |  | Knowledge check. Is deciding to cancel evidence that the original plan failed? | Show answer |  | Remember: Replanning is a driving skill. | Sources | Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §1 | Category B syllabus, chapter 5 | Previous: Protect your attention | Next: Review and self-assessment

cases.subject: M08-L01
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 8. Take responsibility for the vehicle and load | Understand what you may drive |  | Your goal: Use entitlement and vehicle information to assess a car or trailer combination. |  | Requirements. Ordinary category B permits a passenger car or light goods vehicle with a total weight of no more than 3,500 kg. For trailers, either the trailer's total weight is at most 750 kg, or, if above 750 kg, the car and trailer's combined total weights must not exceed 3,500 kg. The first route can therefore permit a combination up to 4,250 kg; it does not mean every 4,250 kg combination is permitted on ordinary B. Category B · Car with trailer |  |  |  | Extended B (B96) permits combined total weights up to 4,250 kg, without increasing the car's 3,500 kg limit. Take responsibility for the vehicle and load | Make the load part of the safety check |  | Your goal: Distinguish weight terms and assess securing, capacity and trailer suitability. |  |  | Term |  | Tjänstevikt |  | Meaning for this lesson |  | Vehicle in its defined ready-for-use state; a car's figure includes the driver, while a trailer's does not include cargo. |  |  | Term |  | Totalvikt |  | Meaning for this lesson |  | Registered maximum weight, built from the defined unladen/ready weight and maximum load. |  |  | Term |  | Bruttovikt |  | Meaning for this lesson |  | Actual weight transmitted to the road at that time. |  |  | Term |  | Maximilast |  | Meaning for this lesson |  | Total weight minus the defined ready weight: the maximum passenger/cargo load. |  | Use the official definitions when reading registration data. Weight definitions |  |  | Weight restrictions and vehicle symbols These are independent reference examples. cases.subject: M08-L03
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 8. Take responsibility for the vehicle and load | Keep the car legally ready |  | Your goal: Build an ownership checklist for registration, insurance, inspection and vehicle status. |  | Requirements. The registered owner of an on-road car must have compulsory motor insurance. Not using the car, or having a defect or driving prohibition, does not by itself end that obligation; formal off-road status matters. Compulsory insurance covers specified traffic injuries and damage to others, not every loss to your own car. Optional cover varies by policy. Compulsory motor insurance |  |  | For an ordinary car or light goods vehicle up to 3,500 kg, the normal inspection sequence is: first by 36 months after the month of first use, second by 24 months after the first inspection month, then by 14 months after the preceding inspection month. Check the recorded date and any special category or exemption for your vehicle. An earlier inspection changes the next calculation; an old reminder is not proof of the current deadline. Inspection intervals |  |  | An on-road registration status, valid insurance and completed inspection answer different questions. Check the vehicle's status and any prohibition before use, and deal with tax obligations through the current official service. A car being physically driveable does not establish legal readiness. On-road and off-road status |  |  | Ownership process. Transportstyrelsen currently provides eligible private-person transfers through Mina sidor; other cases may require the latest registration certificate part 2. The service has eligibility conditions. Consult the current instructions instead of relying on an old app or a remembered screen sequence. Part 1 and the vehicle enquiry service provide technical information; protect ownership documents appropriately. Ownership transfer · Registration certificate |  |  |  | Resolve a missed inspection |  | Inspection deadline · An automatic ban. If the required periodic inspection deadline is missed, an automatic driving ban (inträtt körförbud) applies. You remain responsible even without a reminder. Booking a later appointment does not end the ban. The deadline ban lasts until the inspection has been carried out; follow its result, since defects can bring a new prohibition or a repair/reinspection requirement. Check the vehicle record before ordinary use. Transportstyrelsen: missed inspection · Vehicle Regulation, chapter 6 §§15–21 |  |  |  | Restricted trips. With an overdue-inspection ban and on-road status (påställd), only the shortest suitable route to a repair workshop for repair or to an inspection business for inspection is permitted. If the vehicle is off-road (avställd) and the ban still applies, the exception is the shortest suitable route to the nearest inspection business. Traffic insurance and other applicable requirements still matter; the off-road exception requires no unpaid vehicle taxes. It does not permit errands or commuting. A prohibition issued because the vehicle is dangerously defective has different conditions: it must be recovered from the place where that prohibition is issued. Transportstyrelsen: inspection prohibitions · Transportstyrelsen: off-road inspection conditions |  |  |  | Worked deadline. An ordinary light car's recorded inspection deadline is 31 October 2026. Without the required inspection, the deadline ban starts on 1 November. An appointment on 5 November does not allow normal driving on 2 November. Arrange a permitted inspection trip, or transport if it cannot be driven safely and lawfully, then follow the inspection result. These dates illustrate the rule; use the actual vehicle's record. Vehicle Regulation, chapter 6 §§15 and 21 |  |  | Worked decision. A buyer collects an on-road car but assumes the seller's insurance is enough for the trip home. The buyer checks the transfer and arranges the required cover from the applicable ownership date before driving. The sale does not transfer the seller's insurance as personal cover for the buyer. |  | Check your understanding |  |  | Knowledge check. (1) Does garaging an on-road car automatically end compulsory insurance? (2) The inspection deadline passed, but you booked an appointment. May you commute meanwhile? | Show answer |  | Remember: Keep a record of dates and obligations, then verify them against the current vehicle record. | Sources | Kontrollbesiktning av personbil och lastbil som inte överstiger 3500 kg i totalvikt - Transportstyrelsen | Besiktning av fordon | Vehicle Regulation (2009:211) | Ställa av ditt fordon | Registreringsbevis - Transportstyrelsen | Trafikförsäkring - Transportstyrelsen | Ägarbyte av fordon - Transportstyrelsen | Ställ av eller på ditt fordon - Transportstyrelsen | Previous: Make the load part of the safety check | Next: Know what assistance cannot do

cases.subject: M08-L03/teaching-010/answer
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 8. Take responsibility for the vehicle and load | Keep the car legally ready |  | Your goal: Build an ownership checklist for registration, insurance, inspection and vehicle status. |  | Requirements. The registered owner of an on-road car must have compulsory motor insurance. Not using the car, or having a defect or driving prohibition, does not by itself end that obligation; formal off-road status matters. Compulsory insurance covers specified traffic injuries and damage to others, not every loss to your own car. Optional cover varies by policy. Compulsory motor insurance |  |  | For an ordinary car or light goods vehicle up to 3,500 kg, the normal inspection sequence is: first by 36 months after the month of first use, second by 24 months after the first inspection month, then by 14 months after the preceding inspection month. Check the recorded date and any special category or exemption for your vehicle. An earlier inspection changes the next calculation; an old reminder is not proof of the current deadline. Inspection intervals |  |  | An on-road registration status, valid insurance and completed inspection answer different questions. Check the vehicle's status and any prohibition before use, and deal with tax obligations through the current official service. A car being physically driveable does not establish legal readiness. On-road and off-road status |  |  | Ownership process. Transportstyrelsen currently provides eligible private-person transfers through Mina sidor; other cases may require the latest registration certificate part 2. The service has eligibility conditions. Consult the current instructions instead of relying on an old app or a remembered screen sequence. Part 1 and the vehicle enquiry service provide technical information; protect ownership documents appropriately. Ownership transfer · Registration certificate |  |  |  | Resolve a missed inspection |  | Inspection deadline · An automatic ban. If the required periodic inspection deadline is missed, an automatic driving ban (inträtt körförbud) applies. You remain responsible even without a reminder. Booking a later appointment does not end the ban. The deadline ban lasts until the inspection has been carried out; follow its result, since defects can bring a new prohibition or a repair/reinspection requirement. Check the vehicle record before ordinary use. Transportstyrelsen: missed inspection · Vehicle Regulation, chapter 6 §§15–21 |  |  |  | Restricted trips. With an overdue-inspection ban and on-road status (påställd), only the shortest suitable route to a repair workshop for repair or to an inspection business for inspection is permitted. If the vehicle is off-road (avställd) and the ban still applies, the exception is the shortest suitable route to the nearest inspection business. Traffic insurance and other applicable requirements still matter; the off-road exception requires no unpaid vehicle taxes. It does not permit errands or commuting. A prohibition issued because the vehicle is dangerously defective has different conditions: it must be recovered from the place where that prohibition is issued. Transportstyrelsen: inspection prohibitions · Transportstyrelsen: off-road inspection conditions |  |  |  | Worked deadline. An ordinary light car's recorded inspection deadline is 31 October 2026. Without the required inspection, the deadline ban starts on 1 November. An appointment on 5 November does not allow normal driving on 2 November. Arrange a permitted inspection trip, or transport if it cannot be driven safely and lawfully, then follow the inspection result. These dates illustrate the rule; use the actual vehicle's record. Vehicle Regulation, chapter 6 §§15 and 21 |  |  | Worked decision. A buyer collects an on-road car but assumes the seller's insurance is enough for the trip home. The buyer checks the transfer and arranges the required cover from the applicable ownership date before driving. The sale does not transfer the seller's insurance as personal cover for the buyer. |  | Check your understanding |  |  | Knowledge check. (1) Does garaging an on-road car automatically end compulsory insurance? (2) The inspection deadline passed, but you booked an appointment. May you commute meanwhile? | Hide answer |  |  | Answer: (1) No. Formal status and insurance rules apply. (2) No. The automatic deadline ban continues until inspection is carried out. Only the applicable restricted inspection/repair trip is permitted; vehicle status, insurance, tax and safety conditions must be satisfied. Follow the inspection result and check for any further prohibition before ordinary use. |  | Remember: Keep a record of dates and obligations, then verify them against the current vehicle record. | Sources | Kontrollbesiktning av personbil och lastbil som inte överstiger 3500 kg i totalvikt - Transportstyrelsen | Besiktning av fordon | Vehicle Regulation (2009:211) | Ställa av ditt fordon | Registreringsbevis - Transportstyrelsen | Trafikförsäkring - Transportstyrelsen | Ägarbyte av fordon - Transportstyrelsen | Ställ av eller på ditt fordon - Transportstyrelsen | Previous: Make the load part of the safety check | Next: Know what assistance cannot do

cases.subject: M08-L04
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 8. Take responsibility for the vehicle and load | Know what assistance cannot do |  | Your goal: Explain why safety systems and powertrain differences do not remove your duties to observe and control. |  | Trafikverket describes modern protection as including crashworthiness and systems such as lane assistance and automatic emergency braking. These functions can help, but a good safety rating is not a promise that any collision can be avoided. Recent official crash testing also shows the limits of automatic braking in severe truck-trailer collision scenarios. Crash safety · Trafikverket: braking and truck-trailer tests |  |  |  | ABS is anti-lock braking. It helps retain the ability to develop steering and braking forces together, within available friction. Stability control reduces the risk of skid crashes; it does not create extra road grip or excuse excessive speed. The driver still has to maintain control and an appropriate speed. VTI friction report, section 4.3 · Trafikverket: tyre and stability advice · Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §14 |  |  |  |  | Powertrain awareness. A plug-in hybrid can operate on electricity and with a combustion engine. That difference matters when interpreting fuel use and emissions: do not assume that every journey is electrically powered. Transportstyrelsen: plug-in hybrids |  |  | For the actual vehicle, establish how it becomes ready to move, how drive and reverse are selected, how it is secured, and what warnings or assistance limitations need attention. Do not transfer a universal gear-change, engine-speed, coasting or brake-check recipe between manual, automatic, hybrid and electric vehicles. Vehicle-specific procedures need the vehicle's own instructions and practical teaching. The curriculum's role is to help you identify those questions, not guess their answers. |  | Assistance has limits | Side-obstruction marker. cases.subject: M09-L01
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 9. Reduce the impact of each journey | Look beyond the exhaust |  | Your goal: Compare climate, air-quality and noise effects without assuming that a vehicle has no environmental impact. |  | Transportstyrelsen distinguishes several effects. Greenhouse-gas emissions relate to the amount of travel, fuels, energy efficiency and electrification. Air pollution includes exhaust emissions and wear particles from brakes, tyres and the road. Noise is another effect, with tyre-road noise becoming important as speed rises. These are different measures: improving one does not prove that every environmental effect has disappeared. Climate and energy · Air quality · Noise |  |  |  |  | Learning approach. Ask what a comparison includes. Does an emissions figure describe a test result, the actual journey or a broader lifecycle? Are you comparing equal distances and occupancy? If the basis is missing, avoid a confident numerical conclusion. This lesson does not assign a universal emissions saving to a powertrain or declare a whole journey “zero impact.” |  | A plug-in hybrid combines electrical and combustion-engine operation. Transportstyrelsen changed the weighting used for new registrations in 2026 to better reflect the mix of those modes. The general lesson is to understand what a reported figure represents; it is not a promise about your next journey's consumption. Transportstyrelsen: plug-in-hybrid weighting |  |  | Understand emissions |  | Emissions explained · Fossil carbon and a cold catalyst. Fossil petrol contains carbon stored for millions of years. Burning it combines that carbon with oxygen and releases CO₂ into the atmosphere. The added CO₂ strengthens the natural greenhouse effect and contributes to warming. Long-stored carbon: Naturvårdsverket · Climate effect: Trafikverket |  |  |  | A conventional petrol car's three-way catalyst reduces carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides by chemical conversion. It needs sufficient heat to become effective, so it is least effective just after a cold start. Conversion products include water and CO₂: cleaning up these pollutants does not capture the fossil carbon or cancel its climate impact. No single warm-up time applies to every car. Transportstyrelsen: catalyst operation, page 24 · Trafikverket: cold emission controls |  |  |  | Pollutant comparison. Keep CO distinct from CO₂. The table summarises different mechanisms; one cleaner exhaust measure cannot stand for all of them. |  |  | Substance |  | CO₂ · carbon dioxide |  | Why it matters |  | Added fossil CO₂ strengthens the greenhouse effect. |  |  | Substance |  | CO · carbon monoxide |  | Why it matters |  | Binds strongly to haemoglobin and interferes with the blood's oxygen transport. |  |  | Substance |  | NOx · nitrogen oxides |  | Why it matters |  | Can irritate airways, contribute to acidification and, with hydrocarbons and sunlight, form ground-level ozone. |  |  | Substance |  | Traffic particles |  | Why it matters |  | Exhaust and wear particles can enter and harm the respiratory system. |  | Trafikverket: CO, NOx and particle mechanisms · Trafikverket: CO₂ and warming |  |  |  | Compare powertrains and washing |  | Powertrain and washing · Check the boundary. A battery-electric car uses only electricity for propulsion and has no combustion tailpipe exhaust while driving. That does not remove impacts from vehicle/battery production, raw-material extraction or electricity supply. Tyre and road wear still matter. A plug-in hybrid combines electric and combustion operation and its traction battery can be charged externally. A conventional non-plug-in hybrid cannot be charged from an external electricity supply. Trafikverket: electric cars and hybrid types |  |  | Choose a purpose-built automatic or self-service wash that collects and treats its wastewater. Washing on an ordinary street or driveway can carry oil, metals and cleaning chemicals into ground or surface water. Treatment reduces the problem but does not remove every pollutant. Follow the facility's product instructions and local water-protection rules. Göteborg environmental authority: washing and treatment |  |  | Apply the comparison. A catalyst-equipped petrol car still releases fossil CO₂. An electric car avoids combustion exhaust on that drive, but needs a broader production-and-energy comparison. For either car, choose washing by how the dirty water is handled, rather than assuming a mild detergent makes street runoff harmless. |  | Worked decision. Two vehicles are advertised using different environmental measures. One figure describes exhaust emissions under a test procedure; another describes noise. The learner does not rank them as though both figures measure the same thing. They first identify the question being answered and the information still missing. |  | Check your understanding |  |  | Knowledge check. (1) Why does fossil petrol warm the climate, even with a catalyst, and when is that catalyst least effective? (2) Match CO, NOx and particles to their effects. (3) Does an electric car have no environmental impact; which hybrid can charge externally? (4) Where should washing water go? | Show answer |  | Remember: Name the effect and the basis of comparison before making the claim. | Sources | Kolets kretslopp rubbas | Hastighet och hållbarhet | Åtgärder mot manipulering av viss fordonsutrustning – avgasrening och vägmätare | Vägtrafikens luftföroreningar | Tvätta bilen rätt | Buller  - Transportstyrelsen | Elfordon – så funkar det | Förändrad viktningsfaktor för nya laddhybrider | Klimat och energi - Transportstyrelsen | Luftkvalitet  - Transportstyrelsen | Previous: Reduce the impact of each journey | Next: Use energy with foresight

cases.subject: M09-L02
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 9. Reduce the impact of each journey | Use energy with foresight |  | Your goal: Plan anticipatory driving that reduces unnecessary energy use while preserving safety. |  | Transportstyrelsen recommends correct tyre pressure, observing speed limits and removing unused roof racks or roof boxes. Driving technique and environmental awareness are part of driver education and assessment. Transportstyrelsen: economical driving |  |  | Learning approach. Look ahead and respond early to a developing queue rather than accelerating towards it and then braking sharply. Choose a suitable speed and preserve a gap that lets you adapt smoothly. This is not an instruction to delay necessary braking: safe control and traffic duties come first. If you need to stop for a person, do so regardless of what an efficiency display suggests. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§2 and 14 |  |  | Prepare the vehicle for the trip. Check the specified tyre pressure and remove unnecessary external carrying equipment when it is no longer needed. Combine these habits with realistic route and timing decisions. Avoid claiming a fixed percentage saving: load, road, weather, vehicle and technique all affect the outcome. |  | Vehicle-specific boundary. Gear selection and deceleration strategies vary. Do not use a fixed engine-speed rule for every car or assume every powertrain cuts fuel or recovers energy in the same way. Learn the actual vehicle's approved operation with your instructor. This book does not recommend coasting in neutral or switching the vehicle off while moving. |  | Use energy with control |  | Practical energy choices · Prepare and control the car. Use a timer with an installed electric engine heater so it warms the engine when needed, without running unnecessarily long. Set it for the intended departure using the equipment instructions and conditions; there is no universal heating duration. Gagnef municipal energy advice: heater timer |  |  | Air conditioning consumes energy, but it can support comfort, alertness and clear windows. Avoid unnecessary cooling while keeping those safety benefits. Use the car's appropriate demisting controls; visibility takes priority over a saving. Cooling is not a remedy for sleep deprivation: stop and rest if drowsy. Revisit M07-L01 for seeing clearly and M07-L03 for attention. NZ Transport Agency: cooling, alertness and demisting |  |  |  |  | In a conventional manual car, choose a suitably high gear in which the engine runs smoothly without labouring. Change down if the load or gradient makes that gear unsuitable. Engine braking means slowing with the accelerator released while a suitable gear remains engaged; do not disengage the drive by pressing the clutch or selecting neutral for this technique. Use the brakes whenever safety requires. Actual engine control varies, so this definition does not promise zero fuel use or a universal RPM. Official vehicle agency: comfortable gear choice and in-gear deceleration |  |  | Unnecessary carried mass increases the demands on the vehicle. Unload heavy equipment you no longer need before future journeys, while retaining necessary safety and access equipment. Removing cargo is a different check from removing a roof box's air resistance. Swedish public energy advice: minimise weight |  |  | Apply before departure. Remove unused heavy equipment, schedule the heater for the trip, and keep effective demisting. On an uphill section, use the gear the car can comfortably handle; a high gear that strains the engine is not the intended economical technique. |  | Calculate journey consumption and savings |  | Fuel arithmetic · Understand the unit. A consumption rate of 6.5 litres per 100 km means 6.5 litres for each 100 km under the supplied or measured conditions. A 200 km journey at the same assumed rate uses twice as much, while 50 km uses half as much. Actual consumption varies with vehicle, load, road, weather and driving. Transportstyrelsen: economical driving supplies the driving context; the equations below are editorial arithmetic derived from the unit, not agency-prescribed formulas. |  |  | Journey consumption: journey litres = distance in km × consumption in litres/100 km ÷ 100. Divide distance by 100 to find the number of 100 km portions, then multiply by the supplied rate. The kilometres cancel, leaving litres. Retain decimal working and round only the final result at the precision requested. |  | Consumption example · 120 km at 6.5 litres/100 km. The journey contains 120 ÷ 100 = 1.2 portions of 100 km. Consumption = 1.2 × 6.5 = 7.8 litres. Do not multiply distance by the rate without dividing by 100; that would misread the unit. |  | Savings from a supplied reduction: litres saved = distance in km × reduction in litres/100 km ÷ 100. If two consumption rates are supplied, subtract the lower rate from the higher first. Multiply that difference by the number of 100 km portions. A supplied saving is an exercise assumption, not a guaranteed benefit of a particular driving technique. |  | Savings example · A reduction of 1.5 litres/100 km over 300 km. The journey has 300 ÷ 100 = 3 portions. Savings = 3 × 1.5 = 4.5 litres. This is the difference in litres used, not the new total consumption. You need the original or new consumption rate to calculate either total. |  | Two-rate example · 7.0 and 6.5 litres/100 km over 240 km. First find the rate difference: 7.0 − 6.5 = 0.5 litres/100 km. Savings = 240 × 0.5 ÷ 100 = 1.2 litres. The original journey uses 16.8 litres and the lower-rate journey 15.6 litres; their difference is also 1.2 litres. No percentage-saving promise is implied. |  | Exact values and displayed answers |  | Precision and midpoint rounding · Keep the exact result visible. Some supplied savings exercises display one-decimal answers without specifying precision or a rounding convention in their prompts. Four such examples below use ties-to-even for the displayed keyed value. This rounds to the nearest tenth; at an exact halfway value, choose the tenth whose retained digit is even. It differs from rounding a halfway value upwards. Do not call a rounded value the exact amount, or silently apply one convention where another is intended. |  | Four midpoint examples. A reduction of 0.5 litres/100 km over 150 km gives exactly 0.75 litres, displayed as 0.8 to one decimal using ties-to-even. A reduction of 1.5 over 150 km gives exactly 2.25 litres, displayed as 2.2. A reduction of 0.5 over 250 km gives exactly 1.25 litres, displayed as 1.2. A reduction of 1.5 over 250 km gives exactly 3.75 litres, displayed as 3.8. The units for every reduction are litres/100 km. |  | Compare conventions. With ordinary half-up rounding to one decimal, 2.25 becomes 2.3 and 1.25 becomes 1.3; ties-to-even gives 2.2 and 1.2. The exact products remain 2.25 and 1.25 litres. For these supplied examples, keep the exact arithmetic and the disclosed displayed-answer convention separate. For a new problem, follow its stated precision/convention; if they are absent, report the exact result and recognise that a rounded answer needs an assumption. Round once at the end, not the rate or intermediate product. |  | Try the fuel arithmetic. (A) Find journey consumption for 80 km at 6.5 litres/100 km. (B) Find the saving from a supplied reduction of 0.5 litres/100 km over 250 km, first exactly and then to one decimal using ties-to-even. (C) Find the saving over 200 km when supplied consumption falls from 7.5 to 6.2 litres/100 km. Give your units and show the rate difference where needed. Answers are in the separate lesson answer section. |  | Look ahead and preserve room | The teal car approaches a queue on the right side of the road. Look ahead, retain room to stop and keep the crossing clear. The illustration does not specify a measured following distance. |  | The teal car approaches a queue on the right side of the road. Look ahead, retain room to stop and keep the crossing clear. The illustration does not specify a measured following distance. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked decision. You can see that a traffic queue is stationary ahead. You check behind and begin a controlled reduction in speed early, retaining enough room to stop. You do not accelerate simply to close the gap, and you do not roll into a crossing to preserve momentum. |  | Check your understanding |  |  | Knowledge check. (1) May economy override a necessary stop? (2) How should you use an engine-heater timer and cooling? (3) What is a suitable high gear and engine braking in a manual car? (4) What should happen to unneeded heavy cargo? (5) Complete the three fuel-arithmetic exercises above, including exact and rounded values for B. | Show answer |  | Remember: Reduce avoidable demands on the car while keeping full control of the journey. | Sources | Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §1 | Energi- och klimatrådgivning | Sparsam körning | Features that affect the environment | Fuel efficient driving tips | Sparsam körning | Previous: Look beyond the exhaust | Next: Choose the journey as well as the car

Look ahead and respond early to a developing queue rather than accelerating towards it and then braking sharply. Choose a suitable speed and preserve a gap that lets you adapt smoothly. This is not an instruction to delay necessary braking: safe control and traffic duties come first. If you need to stop for a person, do so regardless of what an efficiency display suggests. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§2 and 14 |  |  | Prepare the vehicle for the trip. Check the specified tyre pressure and remove unnecessary external carrying equipment when it is no longer needed. Combine these habits with realistic route and timing decisions. Avoid claiming a fixed percentage saving: load, road, weather, vehicle and technique all affect the outcome. |  | Vehicle-specific boundary. Gear selection and deceleration strategies vary. Do not use a fixed engine-speed rule for every car or assume every powertrain cuts fuel or recovers energy in the same way. Learn the actual vehicle's approved operation with your instructor. This book does not recommend coasting in neutral or switching the vehicle off while moving. |  | Use energy with control |  | Practical energy choices · Prepare and control the car. Use a timer with an installed electric engine heater so it warms the engine when needed, without running unnecessarily long. Set it for the intended departure using the equipment instructions and conditions; there is no universal heating duration. Change down if the load or gradient makes that gear unsuitable. A consumption rate of 6.5 litres per 100 km means 6.5 litres for each 100 km under the supplied or measured conditions. A 200 km journey at the same assumed rate uses twice as much, while 50 km uses half as much. Actual consumption varies with vehicle, load, road, weather and driving. This is not an instruction to delay necessary braking: safe control and traffic duties come first. If you need to stop for a person, do so regardless of what an efficiency display suggests. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§2 and 14 |  |  | Prepare the vehicle for the trip. Check the specified tyre pressure and remove unnecessary external carrying equipment when it is no longer needed. Combine these habits with realistic route and timing decisions. Avoid claiming a fixed percentage saving: load, road, weather, vehicle and technique all affect the outcome. |  | Vehicle-specific boundary. Gear selection and deceleration strategies vary. Do not use a fixed engine-speed rule for every car or assume every powertrain cuts fuel or recovers energy in the same way. Learn the actual vehicle's approved operation with your instructor. This book does not recommend coasting in neutral or switching the vehicle off while moving. |  | Use energy with control |  | Practical energy choices · Prepare and control the car. Use a timer with an installed electric engine heater so it warms the engine when needed, without running unnecessarily long. Set it for the intended departure using the equipment instructions and conditions; there is no universal heating duration. Gagnef municipal energy advice: heater timer |  |  | Air conditioning consumes energy, but it can support comfort, alertness and clear windows. Avoid unnecessary cooling while keeping those safety benefits. Use the car's appropriate demisting controls; visibility takes priority over a saving. Cooling is not a remedy for sleep deprivation: stop and rest if drowsy. Revisit M07-L01 for seeing clearly and M07-L03 for attention. NZ Transport Agency: cooling, alertness and demisting |  |  |  |  | In a conventional manual car, choose a suitably high gear in which the engine runs smoothly without labouring. Change down if the load or gradient makes that gear unsuitable. Engine braking means slowing with the accelerator released while a suitable gear remains engaged; do not disengage the drive by pressing the clutch or selecting neutral for this technique. Use the brakes whenever safety requires. Actual engine control varies, so this definition does not promise zero fuel use or a universal RPM. Official vehicle agency: comfortable gear choice and in-gear deceleration |  |  | Unnecessary carried mass increases the demands on the vehicle. Unload heavy equipment you no longer need before future journeys, while retaining necessary safety and access equipment. Removing cargo is a different check from removing a roof box's air resistance. Swedish public energy advice: minimise weight |  |  | Apply before departure. Remove unused heavy equipment, schedule the heater for the trip, and keep effective demisting. On an uphill section, use the gear the car can comfortably handle; a high gear that strains the engine is not the intended economical technique. |  | Calculate journey consumption and savings |  | Fuel arithmetic · Understand the unit. A consumption rate of 6.5 litres per 100 km means 6.5 litres for each 100 km under the supplied or measured conditions. A 200 km journey at the same assumed rate uses twice as much, while 50 km uses half as much. Actual consumption varies with vehicle, load, road, weather and driving. Transportstyrelsen: economical driving supplies the driving context; the equations below are editorial arithmetic derived from the unit, not agency-prescribed formulas. |  |  | Journey consumption: journey litres = distance in km × consumption in litres/100 km ÷ 100. Divide distance by 100 to find the number of 100 km portions, then multiply by the supplied rate. The kilometres cancel, leaving litres. Retain decimal working and round only the final result at the precision requested. |  | Consumption example · 120 km at 6.5 litres/100 km. The journey contains 120 ÷ 100 = 1.2 portions of 100 km. Consumption = 1.2 × 6.5 = 7.8 litres. Do not multiply distance by the rate without dividing by 100; that would misread the unit. |  | Savings from a supplied reduction: litres saved = distance in km × reduction in litres/100 km ÷ 100. If two consumption rates are supplied, subtract the lower rate from the higher first. Multiply that difference by the number of 100 km portions. A supplied saving is an exercise assumption, not a guaranteed benefit of a particular driving technique. |  | Savings example · A reduction of 1.5 litres/100 km over 300 km. The journey has 300 ÷ 100 = 3 portions. Savings = 3 × 1.5 = 4.5 litres. This is the difference in litres used, not the new total consumption. You need the original or new consumption rate to calculate either total. |  | Two-rate example · 7.0 and 6.5 litres/100 km over 240 km. First find the rate difference: 7.0 − 6.5 = 0.5 litres/100 km. Savings = 240 × 0.5 ÷ 100 = 1.2 litres. The original journey uses 16.8 litres and the lower-rate journey 15.6 litres; their difference is also 1.2 litres. No percentage-saving promise is implied. |  | Exact values and displayed answers |  | Precision and midpoint rounding · Keep the exact result visible. Some supplied savings exercises display one-decimal answers without specifying precision or a rounding convention in their prompts. Four such examples below use ties-to-even for the displayed keyed value. This rounds to the nearest tenth; at an exact halfway value, choose the tenth whose retained digit is even. It differs from rounding a halfway value upwards. Do not call a rounded value the exact amount, or silently apply one convention where another is intended. |  | Four midpoint examples. A reduction of 0.5 litres/100 km over 150 km gives exactly 0.75 litres, displayed as 0.8 to one decimal using ties-to-even. A reduction of 1.5 over 150 km gives exactly 2.25 litres, displayed as 2.2. A reduction of 0.5 over 250 km gives exactly 1.25 litres, displayed as 1.2. A reduction of 1.5 over 250 km gives exactly 3.75 litres, displayed as 3.8. The units for every reduction are litres/100 km. |  | Compare conventions. With ordinary half-up rounding to one decimal, 2.25 becomes 2.3 and 1.25 becomes 1.3; ties-to-even gives 2.2 and 1.2. The exact products remain 2.25 and 1.25 litres. For these supplied examples, keep the exact arithmetic and the disclosed displayed-answer convention separate. For a new problem, follow its stated precision/convention; if they are absent, report the exact result and recognise that a rounded answer needs an assumption. Round once at the end, not the rate or intermediate product. |  | Try the fuel arithmetic. (A) Find journey consumption for 80 km at 6.5 litres/100 km. (B) Find the saving from a supplied reduction of 0.5 litres/100 km over 250 km, first exactly and then to one decimal using ties-to-even. (C) Find the saving over 200 km when supplied consumption falls from 7.5 to 6.2 litres/100 km. Give your units and show the rate difference where needed. Answers are in the separate lesson answer section. |  | Look ahead and preserve room | The teal car approaches a queue on the right side of the road. Look ahead, retain room to stop and keep the crossing clear. The illustration does not specify a measured following distance. |  | The teal car approaches a queue on the right side of the road. Look ahead, retain room to stop and keep the crossing clear. The illustration does not specify a measured following distance. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked decision. You can see that a traffic queue is stationary ahead. You check behind and begin a controlled reduction in speed early, retaining enough room to stop. You do not accelerate simply to close the gap, and you do not roll into a crossing to preserve momentum. |  | Check your understanding |  |  | Knowledge check. (1) May economy override a necessary stop? (2) How should you use an engine-heater timer and cooling? (3) What is a suitable high gear and engine braking in a manual car? (4) What should happen to unneeded heavy cargo? (5) Complete the three fuel-arithmetic exercises above, including exact and rounded values for B. | Show answer |  | Remember: Reduce avoidable demands on the car while keeping full control of the journey. | Sources | Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §1 | Energi- och klimatrådgivning | Sparsam körning | Features that affect the environment | Fuel efficient driving tips | Sparsam körning | Previous: Look beyond the exhaust | Next: Choose the journey as well as the car

Look ahead and respond early to a developing queue rather than accelerating towards it and then braking sharply. Choose a suitable speed and preserve a gap that lets you adapt smoothly. This is not an instruction to delay necessary braking: safe control and traffic duties come first. If you need to stop for a person, do so regardless of what an efficiency display suggests. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§2 and 14 |  |  | Prepare the vehicle for the trip. Check the specified tyre pressure and remove unnecessary external carrying equipment when it is no longer needed. Combine these habits with realistic route and timing decisions. Avoid claiming a fixed percentage saving: load, road, weather, vehicle and technique all affect the outcome. |  | Vehicle-specific boundary. Gear selection and deceleration strategies vary. Do not use a fixed engine-speed rule for every car or assume every powertrain cuts fuel or recovers energy in the same way. Learn the actual vehicle's approved operation with your instructor. This book does not recommend coasting in neutral or switching the vehicle off while moving. |  | Use energy with control |  | Practical energy choices · Prepare and control the car. Use a timer with an installed electric engine heater so it warms the engine when needed, without running unnecessarily long. Set it for the intended departure using the equipment instructions and conditions; there is no universal heating duration. Gagnef municipal energy advice: heater timer |  |  | Air conditioning consumes energy, but it can support comfort, alertness and clear windows. Avoid unnecessary cooling while keeping those safety benefits. Use the car's appropriate demisting controls; visibility takes priority over a saving. Cooling is not a remedy for sleep deprivation: stop and rest if drowsy. Revisit M07-L01 for seeing clearly and M07-L03 for attention. NZ Transport Agency: cooling, alertness and demisting |  |  |  |  | In a conventional manual car, choose a suitably high gear in which the engine runs smoothly without labouring. Change down if the load or gradient makes that gear unsuitable. Engine braking means slowing with the accelerator released while a suitable gear remains engaged; do not disengage the drive by pressing the clutch or selecting neutral for this technique. Use the brakes whenever safety requires. Actual engine control varies, so this definition does not promise zero fuel use or a universal RPM. Official vehicle agency: comfortable gear choice and in-gear deceleration |  |  | Unnecessary carried mass increases the demands on the vehicle. Unload heavy equipment you no longer need before future journeys, while retaining necessary safety and access equipment. Removing cargo is a different check from removing a roof box's air resistance. Swedish public energy advice: minimise weight |  |  | Apply before departure. Remove unused heavy equipment, schedule the heater for the trip, and keep effective demisting. On an uphill section, use the gear the car can comfortably handle; a high gear that strains the engine is not the intended economical technique. |  | Calculate journey consumption and savings |  | Fuel arithmetic · Understand the unit. A consumption rate of 6.5 litres per 100 km means 6.5 litres for each 100 km under the supplied or measured conditions. A 200 km journey at the same assumed rate uses twice as much, while 50 km uses half as much. Actual consumption varies with vehicle, load, road, weather and driving. Transportstyrelsen: economical driving supplies the driving context; the equations below are editorial arithmetic derived from the unit, not agency-prescribed formulas. |  |  | Journey consumption: journey litres = distance in km × consumption in litres/100 km ÷ 100. Divide distance by 100 to find the number of 100 km portions, then multiply by the supplied rate. The kilometres cancel, leaving litres. Retain decimal working and round only the final result at the precision requested. |  | Consumption example · 120 km at 6.5 litres/100 km. The journey contains 120 ÷ 100 = 1.2 portions of 100 km. Consumption = 1.2 × 6.5 = 7.8 litres. Do not multiply distance by the rate without dividing by 100; that would misread the unit. |  | Savings from a supplied reduction: litres saved = distance in km × reduction in litres/100 km ÷ 100. If two consumption rates are supplied, subtract the lower rate from the higher first. Multiply that difference by the number of 100 km portions. A supplied saving is an exercise assumption, not a guaranteed benefit of a particular driving technique. |  | Savings example · A reduction of 1.5 litres/100 km over 300 km. The journey has 300 ÷ 100 = 3 portions. Savings = 3 × 1.5 = 4.5 litres. This is the difference in litres used, not the new total consumption. You need the original or new consumption rate to calculate either total. |  | Two-rate example · 7.0 and 6.5 litres/100 km over 240 km. First find the rate difference: 7.0 − 6.5 = 0.5 litres/100 km. Savings = 240 × 0.5 ÷ 100 = 1.2 litres. The original journey uses 16.8 litres and the lower-rate journey 15.6 litres; their difference is also 1.2 litres. No percentage-saving promise is implied. |  | Exact values and displayed answers |  | Precision and midpoint rounding · Keep the exact result visible. Some supplied savings exercises display one-decimal answers without specifying precision or a rounding convention in their prompts. Four such examples below use ties-to-even for the displayed keyed value. This rounds to the nearest tenth; at an exact halfway value, choose the tenth whose retained digit is even. It differs from rounding a halfway value upwards. Do not call a rounded value the exact amount, or silently apply one convention where another is intended. |  | Four midpoint examples. A reduction of 0.5 litres/100 km over 150 km gives exactly 0.75 litres, displayed as 0.8 to one decimal using ties-to-even. A reduction of 1.5 over 150 km gives exactly 2.25 litres, displayed as 2.2. A reduction of 0.5 over 250 km gives exactly 1.25 litres, displayed as 1.2. A reduction of 1.5 over 250 km gives exactly 3.75 litres, displayed as 3.8. The units for every reduction are litres/100 km. |  | Compare conventions. With ordinary half-up rounding to one decimal, 2.25 becomes 2.3 and 1.25 becomes 1.3; ties-to-even gives 2.2 and 1.2. The exact products remain 2.25 and 1.25 litres. For these supplied examples, keep the exact arithmetic and the disclosed displayed-answer convention separate. For a new problem, follow its stated precision/convention; if they are absent, report the exact result and recognise that a rounded answer needs an assumption. A 200 km journey at the same assumed rate uses twice as much, while 50 km uses half as much. Actual consumption varies with vehicle, load, road, weather and driving. Retain decimal working and round only the final result at the precision requested. |  | Consumption example · 120 km at 6.5 litres/100 km. The journey contains 120 ÷ 100 = 1.2 portions of 100 km. Avoid claiming a fixed percentage saving: load, road, weather, vehicle and technique all affect the outcome. |  | Vehicle-specific boundary. Gear selection and deceleration strategies vary. Do not use a fixed engine-speed rule for every car or assume every powertrain cuts fuel or recovers energy in the same way. Learn the actual vehicle's approved operation with your instructor. This book does not recommend coasting in neutral or switching the vehicle off while moving. |  | Use energy with control |  | Practical energy choices · Prepare and control the car. Use a timer with an installed electric engine heater so it warms the engine when needed, without running unnecessarily long. Set it for the intended departure using the equipment instructions and conditions; there is no universal heating duration. Gagnef municipal energy advice: heater timer |  |  | Air conditioning consumes energy, but it can support comfort, alertness and clear windows. Avoid unnecessary cooling while keeping those safety benefits. Use the car's appropriate demisting controls; visibility takes priority over a saving. Cooling is not a remedy for sleep deprivation: stop and rest if drowsy. Revisit M07-L01 for seeing clearly and M07-L03 for attention. NZ Transport Agency: cooling, alertness and demisting |  |  |  |  | In a conventional manual car, choose a suitably high gear in which the engine runs smoothly without labouring. Change down if the load or gradient makes that gear unsuitable. Engine braking means slowing with the accelerator released while a suitable gear remains engaged; do not disengage the drive by pressing the clutch or selecting neutral for this technique. Use the brakes whenever safety requires. Actual engine control varies, so this definition does not promise zero fuel use or a universal RPM. Official vehicle agency: comfortable gear choice and in-gear deceleration |  |  | Unnecessary carried mass increases the demands on the vehicle. Unload heavy equipment you no longer need before future journeys, while retaining necessary safety and access equipment. Removing cargo is a different check from removing a roof box's air resistance. Swedish public energy advice: minimise weight |  |  | Apply before departure. Remove unused heavy equipment, schedule the heater for the trip, and keep effective demisting. On an uphill section, use the gear the car can comfortably handle; a high gear that strains the engine is not the intended economical technique. |  | Calculate journey consumption and savings |  | Fuel arithmetic · Understand the unit. A consumption rate of 6.5 litres per 100 km means 6.5 litres for each 100 km under the supplied or measured conditions. A 200 km journey at the same assumed rate uses twice as much, while 50 km uses half as much. Actual consumption varies with vehicle, load, road, weather and driving. Transportstyrelsen: economical driving supplies the driving context; the equations below are editorial arithmetic derived from the unit, not agency-prescribed formulas. |  |  | Journey consumption: journey litres = distance in km × consumption in litres/100 km ÷ 100. Divide distance by 100 to find the number of 100 km portions, then multiply by the supplied rate. The kilometres cancel, leaving litres. Retain decimal working and round only the final result at the precision requested. |  | Consumption example · 120 km at 6.5 litres/100 km. The journey contains 120 ÷ 100 = 1.2 portions of 100 km. Consumption = 1.2 × 6.5 = 7.8 litres. Do not multiply distance by the rate without dividing by 100; that would misread the unit. |  | Savings from a supplied reduction: litres saved = distance in km × reduction in litres/100 km ÷ 100. If two consumption rates are supplied, subtract the lower rate from the higher first. Multiply that difference by the number of 100 km portions. A supplied saving is an exercise assumption, not a guaranteed benefit of a particular driving technique. |  | Savings example · A reduction of 1.5 litres/100 km over 300 km. The journey has 300 ÷ 100 = 3 portions. Savings = 3 × 1.5 = 4.5 litres. This is the difference in litres used, not the new total consumption. You need the original or new consumption rate to calculate either total. |  | Two-rate example · 7.0 and 6.5 litres/100 km over 240 km. First find the rate difference: 7.0 − 6.5 = 0.5 litres/100 km. Savings = 240 × 0.5 ÷ 100 = 1.2 litres. The original journey uses 16.8 litres and the lower-rate journey 15.6 litres; their difference is also 1.2 litres. No percentage-saving promise is implied. |  | Exact values and displayed answers |  | Precision and midpoint rounding · Keep the exact result visible. Some supplied savings exercises display one-decimal answers without specifying precision or a rounding convention in their prompts. Four such examples below use ties-to-even for the displayed keyed value. This rounds to the nearest tenth; at an exact halfway value, choose the tenth whose retained digit is even. It differs from rounding a halfway value upwards. Do not call a rounded value the exact amount, or silently apply one convention where another is intended. |  | Four midpoint examples. A reduction of 0.5 litres/100 km over 150 km gives exactly 0.75 litres, displayed as 0.8 to one decimal using ties-to-even. A reduction of 1.5 over 150 km gives exactly 2.25 litres, displayed as 2.2. A reduction of 0.5 over 250 km gives exactly 1.25 litres, displayed as 1.2. A reduction of 1.5 over 250 km gives exactly 3.75 litres, displayed as 3.8. The units for every reduction are litres/100 km. |  | Compare conventions. With ordinary half-up rounding to one decimal, 2.25 becomes 2.3 and 1.25 becomes 1.3; ties-to-even gives 2.2 and 1.2. The exact products remain 2.25 and 1.25 litres. For these supplied examples, keep the exact arithmetic and the disclosed displayed-answer convention separate. For a new problem, follow its stated precision/convention; if they are absent, report the exact result and recognise that a rounded answer needs an assumption. Round once at the end, not the rate or intermediate product. |  | Try the fuel arithmetic. (A) Find journey consumption for 80 km at 6.5 litres/100 km. (B) Find the saving from a supplied reduction of 0.5 litres/100 km over 250 km, first exactly and then to one decimal using ties-to-even. (C) Find the saving over 200 km when supplied consumption falls from 7.5 to 6.2 litres/100 km. Give your units and show the rate difference where needed. Answers are in the separate lesson answer section. |  | Look ahead and preserve room | The teal car approaches a queue on the right side of the road. Look ahead, retain room to stop and keep the crossing clear. The illustration does not specify a measured following distance. |  | The teal car approaches a queue on the right side of the road. Look ahead, retain room to stop and keep the crossing clear. The illustration does not specify a measured following distance. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked decision. You can see that a traffic queue is stationary ahead. You check behind and begin a controlled reduction in speed early, retaining enough room to stop. You do not accelerate simply to close the gap, and you do not roll into a crossing to preserve momentum. |  | Check your understanding |  |  | Knowledge check. (1) May economy override a necessary stop? (2) How should you use an engine-heater timer and cooling? (3) What is a suitable high gear and engine braking in a manual car? (4) What should happen to unneeded heavy cargo? (5) Complete the three fuel-arithmetic exercises above, including exact and rounded values for B. | Hide answer |  |  | Answer: (1) No. (2) Heat when needed, avoiding unnecessary runtime; retain comfort, alertness and clear windows without needless cooling. (3) Use a gear allowing smooth running without strain. Engine braking releases the accelerator with a suitable gear engaged; brake as needed. No universal RPM or zero-fuel promise. (4) Unload it before future trips; retain necessary equipment. (5) A: 80 × 6.5 ÷ 100 = 5.2 litres. B: 250 × 0.5 ÷ 100 = exactly 1.25 litres; ties-to-even to one decimal gives 1.2 litres. C: the rate difference is 7.5 − 6.2 = 1.3 litres/100 km; 200 × 1.3 ÷ 100 = 2.6 litres saved. These are supplied exercise rates, not guaranteed technique savings. |  | Remember: Reduce avoidable demands on the car while keeping full control of the journey. | Sources | Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §1 | Energi- och klimatrådgivning | Sparsam körning | Features that affect the environment | Fuel efficient driving tips | Sparsam körning | Previous: Look beyond the exhaust | Next: Choose the journey as well as the car

cases.subject: M09-L03
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 9. Reduce the impact of each journey | Choose the journey as well as the car |  | Your goal: Compare combining trips, walking, cycling, public transport and driving for a realistic personal journey. |  | The syllabus includes transport choices and the way personal circumstances influence them. A useful comparison recognises that people's access needs, schedules and available services differ. Category B syllabus, chapters 4–5 |  |  | Learning approach. Start with the purpose: reaching work, collecting goods, accompanying a person or making a visit. Then list workable options. Could two errands be combined? Could a nearby trip be walked or cycled safely? Is public transport available for both directions? If you share a car journey, can everyone use the required protection and travel without creating a rushed schedule? |  | Do not replace one unrealistic assumption with another. A route may be short but inaccessible to a particular person. A service may run outward but not at the return time. A car may solve those needs, while a different choice suits the following day's journey. The exercise is to make the choice deliberately. |  | Combine a practical journey | Separate journeys: home - shop - home, then home - library - home. Combined journey: home - shop - library - home. These are schematic options, not measured routes or a promised saving. Check practical needs and timing. |  | Separate journeys: home - shop - home, then home - library - home. Combined journey: home - shop - library - home. These are schematic options, not measured routes or a promised saving. Check practical needs and timing. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked decision. A learner normally makes two separate drives to the same district. On a day when both appointments can be combined without leaving anyone waiting unsafely, the learner plans one return trip. No exact fuel saving is claimed; the decision avoids a duplicated journey. |  | Check your understanding |  |  | Knowledge check. Is there one transport mode that is automatically best for every journey and every person? | Show answer |  | Remember: Good planning includes asking whether to drive, not only how to drive. | Sources | Category B syllabus, chapter 5 | Previous: Use energy with foresight | Next: Check where the vehicle can go

A useful comparison recognises that people's access needs, schedules and available services differ. Category B syllabus, chapters 4–5 |  |  | Learning approach. Start with the purpose: reaching work, collecting goods, accompanying a person or making a visit. Then list workable options. Could two errands be combined? Could a nearby trip be walked or cycled safely? Is public transport available for both directions? If you share a car journey, can everyone use the required protection and travel without creating a rushed schedule? |  | Do not replace one unrealistic assumption with another. A route may be short but inaccessible to a particular person. A service may run outward but not at the return time. A car may solve those needs, while a different choice suits the following day's journey. The exercise is to make the choice deliberately. |  | Combine a practical journey | Separate journeys: home - shop - home, then home - library - home. Combined journey: home - shop - library - home. These are schematic options, not measured routes or a promised saving. Check practical needs and timing. |  | Separate journeys: home - shop - home, then home - library - home. Combined journey: home - shop - library - home. These are schematic options, not measured routes or a promised saving. Check practical needs and timing. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked decision. A learner normally makes two separate drives to the same district. On a day when both appointments can be combined without leaving anyone waiting unsafely, the learner plans one return trip. No exact fuel saving is claimed; the decision avoids a duplicated journey. |  | Check your understanding |  |  | Knowledge check. Is there one transport mode that is automatically best for every journey and every person? | Show answer |  | Remember: Good planning includes asking whether to drive, not only how to drive. | Sources | Category B syllabus, chapter 5 | Previous: Use energy with foresight | Next: Check where the vehicle can go

cases.subject: M09-L04
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 9. Reduce the impact of each journey | Check where the vehicle can go |  | Your goal: Find official environmental-zone information and determine what to verify before entering. |  | Requirements. Municipalities can introduce environmental zones under the national framework. Class 1 concerns heavy buses and heavy goods vehicles; class 2 concerns passenger cars and light buses/goods vehicles. For class 2, spark-ignition vehicles need Euro 5 or Euro 6 and diesel vehicles need Euro 6. For light vehicles, class 3 ordinarily permits only electric, fuel-cell or qualifying gas vehicles; gas vehicles must meet the specified Euro 6 emissions criteria. A light plug-in hybrid is not admitted merely because it can sometimes run electrically. Exemptions exist for specified vehicles and uses. cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 10. Respond, reflect and keep learning | When the car cannot continue |  | Your goal: Compare a breakdown on an ordinary road, a motorway and in a tunnel. |  | Requirement. If a breakdown leaves a vehicle where stopping is prohibited, it must be moved to a suitable place as soon as possible, subject to the special rules for an accident scene. Warning obligations depend on the situation. A warning triangle must give approaching drivers enough warning; the law does not prescribe one universal distance for every road. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§51 and 57 |  |  | Official motorway/2+1-road advice. If possible, reach the safest available stopping place. Switch on hazard lights, warn other traffic and leave the vehicle and carriageway promptly. Move away from traffic, outside a barrier where one exists. Trafikverket recommends placing the triangle at least 100 m away, preferably farther, and taking care while doing so, walking at the side and outside the barrier where possible. Do not expose yourself in the traffic lane to carry out a roadside repair. Call professional recovery; call 112 when life is in danger. Trafikverket: breakdown advice |  |  | Tunnel advice is different. Use hazard lights, move towards the edge or an emergency bay if possible and switch off the engine. For a non-urgent incident, Trafikverket advises staying in the car or protected from traffic close to it while calling for assistance. In an urgent situation, leave for the nearest emergency exit and use the assistance point, emergency phone or 112. In a fire, leave and reach an emergency exit; follow signs, announcements and emergency personnel. Do not turn a non-urgent-tunnel recommendation into advice to stay beside a fire. Do not assume that a procedure for a sheltered bay, an exposed motorway shoulder and a smoke-filled tunnel can be identical. |  | Keep the hot coolant cap closed |  | Overheating · Leave the hot cap closed. In a conventional pressurised cooling system, hot coolant and steam can remain under pressure even after the engine is switched off. Opening the radiator cap, or the cap of a pressurised coolant reservoir, can release that pressure and expel scalding liquid or steam, causing severe burns. Never loosen or remove the cap while the engine or cooling system is hot. Switching off is not proof that pressure and heat have disappeared. Manufacturer handbook: hot coolant and pressure warning |  |  | Treat a temperature warning as a reason to respond according to the actual vehicle handbook, not as an invitation to open a cap. After reaching the safest available stopping place as conditions allow, follow the vehicle's stopping instructions and this lesson's motorway scene-safety advice. Provide your name, address and information when requested by another involved person or someone whose property was damaged. Notify the owner or police promptly if damaged property has nobody present to receive the information. Notify police promptly for a personal injury that is not insignificant. cases.subject: M10-L03
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 10. Respond, reflect and keep learning | Explain a whole journey |  | Your goal: Review a mixed journey, justify decisions, identify missed hazards and propose safer alternatives. |  | This exercise brings the earlier lessons together. It is an original learning scenario, not an official test question or a court case. |  | Scenario. You plan to take a passenger to a rural appointment using an unfamiliar car. The outward journey includes a residential area, a roundabout and a faster road. Rain is expected later. At the destination, the nearest empty space is before a pedestrian crossing. On the return journey you become delayed; the passenger asks you to pass a slower vehicle near a bend. |  | Work through the decisions. | 1.  |  | Before leaving, establish fitness, entitlement, vehicle readiness, passenger protection and the controls you may need. Check the route and alternatives. | 2.  |  | In the residential area, identify crossings, people hidden by parked vehicles and the applicable speed. At the roundabout, separate entry, lane and exit decisions. | 3.  |  | On the faster section, preserve a following gap and a view ahead. If the weather worsens, reassess both lighting and speed. | 4.  |  | At the destination, apply the stopping restrictions before considering convenience. Choose a lawful place with a safe manoeuvre and passenger exit. | 5.  |  | On the return trip, reject an overtaking attempt without a complete clear path. Change the arrival expectation instead of the safety margin. |  | The rules behind these decisions are explained in M02–M07. The duties to adapt speed, yield where required and avoid dangerous manoeuvres remain applicable throughout. Traffic Regulation, chapters 2–3 |  |  |  |  | Explain the whole journey | Residential area: describe crossings, people near parked vehicles and the appropriate speed. |  | Residential area: describe crossings, people near parked vehicles and the appropriate speed. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. | Roundabout. Three white arrows circulate anticlockwise on blue. | Roundabout: explain entry, lane and exit decisions separately. D3 is an official recognition example; it does not by itself show every entry duty. |  | Roundabout: explain entry, lane and exit decisions separately. D3 is an official recognition example; it does not by itself show every entry duty. |  | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Transportstyrelsen · D3 · official artwork |  | Rain: reassess the view, lighting, speed and following gap as conditions change. |  | Rain: reassess the view, lighting, speed and following gap as conditions change. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. | Traffic and parked vehicles: preserve visibility and room for others. This urban detail does not depict the later rural bend; use the written scenario to assess that decision. |  | Traffic and parked vehicles: preserve visibility and room for others. This urban detail does not depict the later rural bend; use the written scenario to assess that decision. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked reflection. “I noticed the bend but focused on the passenger's request. Next time I will state that I am waiting before I start looking for a gap.” This identifies a trigger and an action. “I must be more careful” does not explain what to practise. |  | Check your understanding |  |  | Knowledge check. If no collision occurred, does that prove every decision was sound? | Show answer |  | Remember: Assess the decision process as well as the outcome. | Sources | Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §1 | Previous: When someone may be hurt | Next: Make a realistic readiness plan

It is an original learning scenario, not an official test question or a court case. |  | Scenario. You plan to take a passenger to a rural appointment using an unfamiliar car. The outward journey includes a residential area, a roundabout and a faster road. Rain is expected later. At the destination, the nearest empty space is before a pedestrian crossing. On the return journey you become delayed; the passenger asks you to pass a slower vehicle near a bend. |  | Work through the decisions. | 1.  |  | Before leaving, establish fitness, entitlement, vehicle readiness, passenger protection and the controls you may need. Check the route and alternatives. | 2.  |  | In the residential area, identify crossings, people hidden by parked vehicles and the applicable speed. At the roundabout, separate entry, lane and exit decisions. | 3.  |  | On the faster section, preserve a following gap and a view ahead. If the weather worsens, reassess both lighting and speed. | 4.  |  | At the destination, apply the stopping restrictions before considering convenience. Choose a lawful place with a safe manoeuvre and passenger exit. | 5.  |  | On the return trip, reject an overtaking attempt without a complete clear path. Change the arrival expectation instead of the safety margin. |  | The rules behind these decisions are explained in M02–M07. The duties to adapt speed, yield where required and avoid dangerous manoeuvres remain applicable throughout. Traffic Regulation, chapters 2–3 |  |  |  |  | Explain the whole journey | Residential area: describe crossings, people near parked vehicles and the appropriate speed. |  | Residential area: describe crossings, people near parked vehicles and the appropriate speed. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. | Roundabout. Three white arrows circulate anticlockwise on blue. | Roundabout: explain entry, lane and exit decisions separately. D3 is an official recognition example; it does not by itself show every entry duty. |  | Roundabout: explain entry, lane and exit decisions separately. D3 is an official recognition example; it does not by itself show every entry duty. |  | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Transportstyrelsen · D3 · official artwork |  | Rain: reassess the view, lighting, speed and following gap as conditions change. |  | Rain: reassess the view, lighting, speed and following gap as conditions change. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. | Traffic and parked vehicles: preserve visibility and room for others. This urban detail does not depict the later rural bend; use the written scenario to assess that decision. |  | Traffic and parked vehicles: preserve visibility and room for others. This urban detail does not depict the later rural bend; use the written scenario to assess that decision. | KörkortGo; built-in imagegen artwork. |  | Worked reflection. “I noticed the bend but focused on the passenger's request. Next time I will state that I am waiting before I start looking for a gap.” This identifies a trigger and an action. “I must be more careful” does not explain what to practise. |  | Check your understanding |  |  | Knowledge check. If no collision occurred, does that prove every decision was sound? | Hide answer |  |  | Answer: No. Review whether the decision depended on luck, another person avoiding you, or a margin you could not justify. |  | Remember: Assess the decision process as well as the outcome. | Sources | Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §1 | Previous: When someone may be hurt | Next: Make a realistic readiness plan

cases.subject: M10-L04
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | 10. Respond, reflect and keep learning | Make a realistic readiness plan |  | Your goal: Compare knowledge, practical performance and confidence, then plan further learning and accessible examination preparation. |  | The official theory test covers vehicle knowledge/manoeuvring, environment, road safety, traffic rules and personal factors. It checks understanding across those areas; memorising the wording of practice questions is not equivalent preparation. The practical test requires you to apply knowledge through vehicle checks, manoeuvres and driving in traffic. Trafikverket: category B tests · Practical test |  |  |  | Current standard theory-test format, checked 1 October 2026: 70 questions, of which 65 count towards the score; at least 52 points are needed to pass; standard time is 50 minutes. These administrative figures can change, so verify them before booking. They are not a recommended pass mark for this book's short learning checks. Trafikverket: theory-test format |  |  | Trafikverket provides language options, including English, and application routes for support such as extended time, oral support or an interpreter where appropriate. Support generally needs approval before the supported test can be booked. Check the current requirements and apply early enough for a decision; do not assume that support can be added at the door. Languages · Test support |  |  |  | Learning approach. Review three kinds of evidence: Can you explain the rule and its exceptions? Can you recognise the situation without a prompt? Can you act safely and consistently during supervised practice? A high confidence rating with little evidence is a learning signal, not a readiness certificate. |  | Write your next practice plan in concrete terms: “Recognise cycle passages after a turn and explain the duty before reaching them,” or “Demonstrate the safety check and explain each defect response.” Revisit errors after a delay and in a changed scenario so that you are practising understanding rather than recognising an answer. |  | Worked decision. A learner answers most checks correctly but still needs reminders to scan at junctions. They continue targeted supervised practice instead of treating their theory score as proof of practical readiness. |  | Check your understanding |  |  | Knowledge check. Can this manuscript or its checks certify that you will pass or are ready to drive alone? | Show answer |  | Remember: Readiness is supported by evidence across knowledge, judgement and practical performance. | Sources | Trafikverket: B tests | Trafikverket: safety check | Teoriprov och yrkesprov med stöd - www.trafikverket.se | Teoriprovet på annat språk - www.trafikverket.se | Previous: Explain a whole journey | Next: Review and self-assessment

cases.subject: appendix-A
cases.text: |  |  | Learning library | Put the learning into practice |  | These are original study checklists. Use the cited lessons for the detailed rules and limitations; a tick does not certify a vehicle or driver as safe. | Before a journey | •  |  | Establish that the driver is legally permitted and actually fit to drive. Resolve uncertainty about fatigue, medication or conditions before leaving. See M01-L01/L02. |  |  | •  |  | Check the route, weather, traffic, realistic timing, stopping opportunities and a fallback option. Include the return journey. See M01-L04 and M07-L04. |  |  | •  |  | Check the vehicle, usable visibility, required lighting and controls. Confirm protection for each passenger. See M02. |  | •  |  | Establish load and trailer limits, coupling and securing if relevant. Verify the vehicle's recorded status and obligations. See M08. |  | •  |  | Prepare navigation and passenger help before moving. Keep attention available for traffic. See M07-L03. |  | While approaching a new situation | 1.  |  | Observe: What can I see, what is hidden and who might enter? | 2.  |  | Identify the duty: Which rule, sign, marking, signal or authorised instruction applies? | 3.  |  | Preserve space: Can I stop or alter the plan without forcing another person to avoid me? | 4.  |  | Communicate: Will others understand my intended movement? | 5.  |  | Recheck: Is the information still true as I begin and complete the action? |  | This is an original learning routine based on the observation, risk and cooperation aims of the category B syllabus. It is not an official test sequence. |  | Before leaving a parked vehicle |  | Check that stopping and parking are permitted at that location, time and for that vehicle. Meet fee, duration and permit conditions. Secure against rolling and unauthorised use. Check for people before opening doors and provide a safe place for passengers to leave. See M05-L03/L04 and the Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§47–55. |  |  |  | Sources | Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §1 | Category B syllabus, chapter 5
